Abstract:
<jats:p>Acoustic Emission (AE) and Guided Ultrasonic Waves (GUWs) are non-destructive testing (NDT) methods in several industrial sectors for, e.g., proof testing and periodic inspection of pressure vessels, storage tanks, pipes or pipelines and leak or corrosion detection. In materials research, AE and GUW are useful for characterizing damage accumulation and microscopic damage mechanisms. AE and GUW also show potential for long-term Structural Health and Condition Monitoring (SHM and CM). With increasing computational power, even online monitoring of industrial manufacturing processes has become feasible. Combined with Artificial Intelligence (AI) for analysis this may soon allow for efficient, automated online process control. AI also plays a role in predictive maintenance and cost optimization. Long-term SHM, CM and process control require sensor integration together with data acquisition equipment and possibly data analysis. This raises the question of the long-term durability of all components of the measurement system. So far, only scant quantitative data are available. This paper presents and discusses selected aspects of the long-term durability of sensor behavior, sensor coupling and measurement hardware and software. The aim is to identify research and development needs for reliable, cost-effective, long-term SHM and CM with AE and GUW under combined mechanical and environmental service loads.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Acoustic coupling agents serve as critical interfacial materials connecting piezoelectric transducers with microfluidic chips in acoustofluidic systems. Their performance directly impacts acoustic wave transmission efficiency, device reusability, and reliability in biomedical applications. Considering the rapidly growing body of research in the field of acoustic microfluidics, this review aims to serve as an all-in-one reference on the role of acoustic coupling agents and relevant considerations pertinent to acoustofluidic devices for anyone working in or seeking to enter the field of disposable acoustofluidic devices. To this end, this review seeks to summarize and categorize key aspects of acoustic couplants in the implementation of acoustofluidic devices by examining their underlying physical mechanisms, material classifications, and core applications of coupling agents in acoustofluidics. Gel-based coupling agents are particularly favored for their long-term stability, high coupling efficiency, and ease of preparation, making them integral to acoustic flow control applications. In practice, coupling agents facilitate microparticle trapping, droplet manipulation, and biosample sorting through acoustic impedance matching and wave mode conversion (e.g., Rayleigh-to-Lamb waves). Their thickness and acoustic properties (sound velocity, attenuation coefficient) further modulate sound field distribution to optimize acoustic radiation forces and thermal effects. However, challenges remain regarding stability (evaporation, thermal degradation) and chip compatibility. Further aspects of research into gel-based agents requiring attention include multilayer coupled designs, dynamic thickness control, and enhancing biocompatibility to advance acoustofluidic technologies in point-of-care diagnostics and high-throughput analysis.

Abstract:
A multi-physical signal correlation analysis method is proposed to identify the different tribological properties of materials. The acoustic emission (AE), contact resistance, and frictional force behaviors during dry sliding between four metals, 45# carbon steel, YG12 carbide, 2A12 aluminum alloy, and H62 brass, have been studied. Both positive and negative correlations between the root mean square of the amplified AE (AE RMS) signal and the frictional coefficient have been found in the experiments. In addition, the AE RMS signal and the contact resistance changed with changing sliding speed and normal load in different ways. The different correlation behaviors have been attributed to diverse tribological states under different experimental conditions due to different material characteristics. The correlation analysis provides a new method of quantitatively identifying the tribological states and the AE sources during frictional interaction. The observed anomalous correlations between the AE signal and frictional coefficient should be properly considered according to the different material properties during industrial friction condition monitoring using AE technology.

Below 500 kHz, most couplants are generally expected to suffice, while higher-frequency measurements may suffer loss of high-frequency spectral content unless a low-viscosity couplant or rigid bond is used. A thin, continuous couplant layer is preferred, but it must be thick enough to fill surface roughness or corrugation. Entrapped voids and uneven or tapered couplant layers can reduce sensitivity or introduce directionality. The couplant or bonding agent should also be compatible with the environment and structure, avoid corrosion, and meet application-specific removal requirements. Abstract:
Over the last decade, acoustic methods, including acoustic emission (AE) and ultrasonic testing (UT), have been increasingly deployed for process diagnostics and health monitoring of electrochemical power devices, including batteries, fuel cells, and water electrolysers. These techniques are non-invasive, highly sensitive, and low-cost, providing a high level of spatial and temporal resolution and practicality. Their application in electrochemical devices is based on identifying changes in acoustic signals emitted from or propagated through materials as a result of physical, structural, and electrochemical changes within the material. These changes in acoustic signals are then correlated to critical processes and the health status of these devices. This review summarises progress in the use of acoustic methods for the process and health monitoring of major electrochemical energy conversion and storage devices. First, the fundamental principles of AE and UT are introduced, and then the application of these acoustic techniques to electrochemical power devices are discussed. Conclusions and perspectives on some of the key challenges and potential commercial and academic applications of the devices are highlighted. It is expected that, with further developments, acoustic techniques will form a key part of the suite of diagnostic techniques routinely used to monitor electrochemical devices across various processes, including fabrication, post-mortem examination and recycle decision support to aid the deployment of these devices in increasingly demanding applications.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive Manufacturing (AM) represents an industrial paradigm shift, surpassing conventional methods by building complex three-dimensional products layer by layer, optimizing weight, customization, and sustainability. However, its widespread industrial adoption is hindered by critical quality challenges such as porosity, excessive surface roughness, and insufficient interlayer adhesion. Within this Industry 4.0 context, the convergence of AM with Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) emerges as a promising solution, enabling real-time defect detection, parameter optimization, and mechanical property prediction through sensor-generated data analysis. This study conducts a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to identify, evaluate, and synthesize AI-based data analysis solutions applied to automated AM processes, focusing on quality assurance and real-time anomaly detection through non-visual signal analysis. Employing PRISMA guidelines, the methodology utilized Scopus and Web of Science databases, culminating in the selection of 91 articles after rigorous screening. Content analysis revealed a predominance of research in metallic materials (60 occurrences), with porosity being the most studied defect (44 occurrences). In polymers (31 occurrences), dimensional deviations (12 occurrences) and nozzle failures (7 occurrences) were most explored. Diverse non-visual sensor technologies were identified, including photodiodes and ultrasound for metals, and accelerometers and temperature sensors for polymers. AI methods, notably Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), demonstrated high effectiveness, with reported efficiencies reaching up to 99.30%, in interpreting these complex signals. This work consolidates current knowledge on multi-sensor and AI-driven strategies, essential for enhancing reliability, reducing waste, and accelerating industrial adoption of AM, while outlining future directions for real-time quality assurance advancement.</jats:p>

The paper reports process-generated AE amplitudes up to 70 dB. The airborne sensor was an Avisoft Bioacoustics CM16/CMPA48AAF-5V, covering 2–200 kHz, mounted above the build plate in a custom holder. The structure-borne sensor was a Vallen Systeme VS370-A3 piezoelectric sensor, covering 150–600 kHz, mounted directly beneath the build plate. The signals were acquired synchronously through an Elsys Instruments TPCE-8S DAQ at 1.25 MHz, with a machine trigger used for process synchronization. No couplant or coupling medium is specified in the provided pages; the text only states that the structure-borne sensor was mounted beneath the build plate. The paper explains that the two sensors provide complementary coverage: airborne sensing is useful for lower-frequency process-state emissions, while structure-borne sensing captures higher-frequency emissions associated with cracking or delamination more effectively.                                                                        iii                                        1. INTRODUCTION


Liquid-fueled rocket motors depend on turbopumps to deliver fuel and oxygen to the combustion
chamber at a very high but finely controlled mtws flow rate. The bearings in certain types of
turbopumps are lubricated and cooled by the flow of liquid oxygen through the bearing assembly.
The bearings on the turbopump shaft are open cage ball bearings of specially seleded alloys
designed to meet the load requirements of turbopump service at speeds of up to 35,000 rpm.

If the surface of a bearing ball or race is subjected to excess wear, the stresses on the bearing
become irregular and the lubricating film of oxygen cannot support the uneven load.  Deteriora-
tion of the bearing begins when the lubricating film breaks down.  The heat  of friction
increases, stress irregularities increase, damage to the bearing becomes more severe, and the
increase in frictional heat continues until the kindling temperature of the metal is reached.
The turbopump is then consumed by fire.  Therefore, integrity of the turbopump bearings is
very important to the operation of a liquid-fueled rocket motor.

To ensure the integrity and reliability of turbopump bearings, the alloys and surface treatments
used in the turbopump bearings are tested for durability under simulated rocket motor service
on the bearing materials tester (BMT) at Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC).  However,
further assurance of bearing integrity and reliability could be realized by continuously monitor-
ing the turbopump bearings on a rocket motor to detect and record any changes in surface
condition that may indicate the onset of bearing failure.

A three-phase research program was initiated by NASA in 1983 to investigate the use of acous-
tic monitoring techniques to detect incipient failure in turbopump bearings.  Two prototype
acoustic coupler probes were designed and evaluated, and four units of the final probe design
were fabricated and delivered to MSFC. Success in this program could lead to development of
an on-board monitor which could detect bearing damage in flight and reduce or eliminate the
need for disassembly after each flight.

This final report reviews the accomplishments of the first two phases and presents the results
of fabrication and testing completed in the final phase of the research program.

bearing balls in rolling contact with the outer race.  The probe contach the bearing race on
the outer radius.  The point of the probe in contact with the bearing race couples the sound
to a piezoelectric element  The piezoelectric element has a primary free resonance at about
640 lrHz due to cross coupling in the element between the radial and the thickness vibration
modes. This cross coupling is strong because the thicknese-to-diameter ratio is near 1.

The output of the probe is conditioned in a preamplifier to remove frequencies below 200 lrHz
and match the high sensor impedance'to a 50-93 ohm coaxial cable. The preamplifier is battery
powered in the prototype configuration to provide isolation from power supply noise and elimi-
nate the possibility of a ground loop between the sensor and the preamplifier power supply.
The preamplifier drives up to 1500 feet of coaxial cable. The cable must be properly terminated
at the data acquisition station.

The system is designed to use low frequency variation of the RMS voltage output of the pre-
amplifier as the primary analysis parameter.  Trends in the RMS output are correlated with
the bearing condition at a given coolant flow and rate of rotation of the bearings.  With all
four bearings of the BMT instrumented, direct comparison from bearing to bearing will increase
the sensitivityto detection of bearing wear or surface deterioration.

The excerpt does not identify or provide specifications for the particular AE sensor models named in the question—MISTRAS PAC D9215, Vallen VS-HT, VS160-NS, VS370, or KRN sensors. It describes general high-temperature sensor designs, including piezoelectric discs or plates and buffer-rod-extension systems. A simple piezoelectric sensor is self-generating, rugged, low-cost, and capable of very high sensitivity, on the order of pico-strains, but its usable temperature is limited by loss of piezoelectric behavior near the ceramic’s Curie temperature, as well as by adhesive and solder failure. The excerpt gives an apparent maximum-use-temperature statement of approximately 200°C for PZT, although the scanned text is corrupted. For substantially hotter environments, buffer rods transmit acoustic signals from the hot region to a temperature-sensitive transducer; stainless-steel rods may be air- or water-cooled. Therefore, this passage cannot establish the temperature ratings, sensitivities, or continuous-operation capability of the named commercial sensors at 200°C or 500°C. Model-specific datasheets or manufacturer documentation would be required, especially because continuous 500°C operation generally depends on the complete sensor assembly, mounting, cabling, cooling, and exposure duration.

                           The composition of the acoustic emission system is shown in Figure 4, mainly in-

                        The remaining components are connected in sequence via coaxial cables to form a complete
                              signal acquisition and processing chain.
                           The AE sensor, which is directly or indirectly coupled to the workpiece, serves as the
                            core component of an AE system for data acquisition. It converts mechanical vibrations
                                  (elastic waves) from the workpiece into electrical signals. The classification of AE sensors
                                    is shown in Figure 5. Based on the wave propagation medium, AE sensors are broadly
                             categorized into air-borne acoustic emission (ABAE) and structure-borne acoustic emission
                         (SBAE) sensors [61,62].

                          As the name suggests, ABAE sensors detect AE signals transmitted through air vibra-
                                 tions. The most common ABAE sensor is the microphone, which offers ease of deployment
                           but generally suffers from limited accuracy. In contrast, SBAE sensors capture waves prop-
                            agating through the structure itself. Primary SBAE sensors include piezoelectric transducer
                          (PZT) AE sensors and optical fiber (OF) AE sensors. The latter can be further classified into
                                fiber Bragg grating (FBG) AE sensors, fiber optic ring (FOR) AE sensors, and Fabry–Perot
                              interferometric (FPI) AE sensors based on their distinct sensing principles [63]. PZT AE sen-
                             sors [64,65] utilize piezoelectric ceramics to transduce elastic waves into electrical signals.
                        They are characterized by high sensitivity, excellent stability, and low cost. However, their
                          performance can be compromised in harsh environments involving strong electromagnetic
                               interference, significant corrosion, or elevated temperatures [66]. FBG sensors operate by
                             detecting shifts in the reflected Bragg wavelength induced by strain variations from elastic
                       waves [67]. The primary detection mechanism of the FBG sensors is not based on changes

                          propagation medium for the acoustic energy, but the FBG fundamentally responds to the
                              resulting mechanical deformation.

## 1. shukla2026acousticemissiondirectionality pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000043)

Acoustic emission directionality of the melt pool in laser powder bed fusion
                         additive manufacturing
 Shivam Shuklaa,b,*, Rik Vaerenberga,b, Milad Hamidi Nasaba,b, Konstantinos Grylliasa,b, Bey
                                       Vranckena,b

           a Department of Mechanical Engineering, KU Leuven, Leuven 3001, Belgium

                                b Flanders Make@KU Leuven, Belgium

Abstract

Vibro-acoustic monitoring has emerged as a promising approach for process monitoring and

control in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). Its high temporal resolution and capability to

capture events occurring on the microsecond scale can assist in developing a comprehensive

understanding of complex melt pool dynamics and laser-material interaction. However, the

physical linkage between the acoustic signal and the process remains a challenge. This work

attempts to uncover the complex mechanism of the LPBF process by understanding acoustic

signals and linking them with the actual physical conditions. A microphone is used to capture

the acoustic emissions (AE) generated from the processing zone. Additionally, an on-axis high-

speed camera is used for melt pool monitoring and spatter tracking. Analyzing AE signals

shows that signal energy fluctuations within the frequency band of 100-250 kHz are influenced

by changes in inherent processing conditions, such as scan direction and the orientation of the

vector sequence direction. These fluctuations are correlated with backward vapor plume, melt

pool asymmetry, and spatter ejection during layer processing. The study further reveals that

during processing, the spatter ejects toward the built side of the layer. As most of the previous

work on the use of acoustic emission monitoring of laser powder bed fusion relied heavily on

machine learning (ML) for regime classification and anomaly detection, correlating acoustic

signals with the actual physical events will add to data labeling by providing complementary

contextual information, thereby enhancing the performance of these models. Additionally, this

contextual information is a prerequisite to be able to advance acoustic monitoring from the

layer level to the more local defect level.

Keywords: Additive manufacturing, Laser powder bed fusion, Acoustic emission monitoring,

Signal processing, Spatter tracking

*Corresponding author: shivam.shukla@kuleuven.be

Present address: Department of Mechanical Engineering, KU Leuven, 3001 Leuven, Belgium1.  Introduction

Additive manufacturing (AM) is an advanced manufacturing process of creating intricate 3D

components, and one of the most common industrial additive manufacturing processes is laser

powder bed fusion (LPBF) [1]. In this process, the CAD design of the component is sliced into

a stack of thin layers of approximately 30-120 𝜇𝑚. The process starts with spreading a thin

layer of powder over the base plate and selectively melting it with a laser along a predefined

path to fuse the powder particles. After the laser scan, another layer of powder is deposited

over the previously melted layer, and the process is repeated until a desired 3D component is

formed [2]. Due to its inherent capability of thin layer deposition and fine laser spot size, the

process can create complex geometries with finer geometrical features that are otherwise

impossible to produce using conventional manufacturing processes.  This rapidly growing

manufacturing technology has shown huge potential applications mainly (but not limited to) in

the medical and aerospace industries [3,4].

   Despite offering several advantages, additive manufacturing processes are usually hampered

by the product quality assurance [4,5]. The most common approach to achieving dense and

defect-free parts is the time-consuming trial and error method. However, any changes in part

geometry, powder condition, or processing condition require further iterations of process

optimization  [6].  Additionally,  the  inherent  complexities  of  laser-material  interaction,

combined with high cooling rates and uneven thermal histories, introduce unpredictable

challenges. These factors can compromise process repeatability, even when using optimized

parameters [7]. This unpredictable nature of the process ultimately results in variations in

mechanical properties and a lack of confidence in the process. As a result, these components

have to undergo quality inspection, and their adaptation is generally subjected to quality

certification to ensure their applicability in the desired domain.

  One of the most widely used non-destructive techniques (NDT) for quality inspection of

metal AM parts is X-ray computed tomography (CT scan) [8,9]. However, this method is

usually costly, time-consuming, computationally demanding, and requires substantial effort in

data analysis. To address these challenges, in-situ process monitoring has emerged as a much

more effective alternative, reducing the reliance on expensive post-process inspection and

becoming an integral part of the LPBF process. Real-time monitoring is not only helpful in

developing a keen understanding of several aspects of the process, but it also provides early-

stage anomaly indication. This allows operators to proactively prevent build failure, therebysaving both time and cost. Several process monitoring techniques are employed in LPBF based

on different signal types, including optical [10–12], thermal [13–15], and acoustic monitoring

[16–19]. Recently, Cai et al. [20] provided a comprehensive review of various monitoring

techniques used in laser-based AM, discussing their advantages and limitations. This paper,

however, focuses specifically on acoustic monitoring in LPBF.

   While vision- and temperature-based monitoring techniques offer valuable insights, they

primarily provide surface-level information. Acoustic monitoring, on the other hand, is cost-

effective and offers the unique capability of potentially capturing volumetric information from

the bulk of the material [21]. The first use of AE monitoring in laser-based processes was

reported in laser welding [22–25], and later expanded to several other processes such as laser

cladding [26], directed energy deposition [27–29] (DED) and recently to LPBF. In the case of

LPBF, the melt pool fluctuations produced by laser material interaction generate transient

elastic waves carrying  critical information associated with melt pool  instabilities, crack

formation, keyhole formation, and collapse [20]. However, these phenomena typically occur

over very short time scales, often within the range of 10-100 μs [30]. AE monitoring, with

higher temporal resolution, offers a prominent method to capture these microscale variations.

Two primary types of AE sensors are used in LPBF: structure-borne acoustic emission (SBAE)

sensors and air-borne acoustic emission (ABAE) sensors. SBAE requires physical contact with

the material and captures acoustic waves transmitted by the solid medium. In contrast, ABAE

sensors are non-contact types and are placed inside the build chamber to capture pressure

variation originating from melt pool fluctuations. Most of the published literature utilized air-

borne AE sensors, possibly due to their easier implementation without extensive hardware

modification. However, several factors such as distance, background noise, and angle from the

processing zone can significantly affect the signal quality.

   One of the key challenges in acoustic monitoring is the complexity of the signal, which

necessitates feature extraction to derive meaningful insights. Most studies on the application

of AE sensing in LPBF leverage time, frequency, and time-frequency feature extraction, often

combined with ML. Extensive research has been conducted on using acoustic monitoring to

assess part quality. A fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensor was used by Wasmer et al.  [31] to

capture acoustic signatures for different part qualities. They utilized a reinforced learning

approach to build a classifier using a wavelet spectrogram as model input. Ye et al. [32]

proposed a defect detection method using airborne microphone data with a deep belief network

(DBN) framework. The proposed framework extracted the hierarchical information from rawsignals, avoiding the need for prior feature extraction and data preprocessing. Similarly, an

SBAE sensor was used by Eschner et al. [33] to classify three different classes of density using

an artificial neural network. They further investigated the effect of geometrical complexity on

model performance and achieved F1 score above 85 %,  if the model was trained for a given

geometrical complexity. Drissi-Daoudi et al. [34] compared the performance of four different

ML algorithms over three different materials for classification between lack of fusion,

conduction, and keyhole regime. All the models had comparable results with classificat

(DBN) framework. The proposed framework extracted the hierarchical information from rawsignals, avoiding the need for prior feature extraction and data preprocessing. Similarly, an

SBAE sensor was used by Eschner et al. [33] to classify three different classes of density using

an artificial neural network. They further investigated the effect of geometrical complexity on

model performance and achieved F1 score above 85 %,  if the model was trained for a given

geometrical complexity. Drissi-Daoudi et al. [34] compared the performance of four different

ML algorithms over three different materials for classification between lack of fusion,

conduction, and keyhole regime. All the models had comparable results with classification

accuracy above 90 %. The study also revealed that acoustic signatures are unique to a material

and a universal machine learning model is not feasible. Moreover, conventional supervised

machine learning models rely on balanced datasets across all classes to perform reliably. To

overcome  this  limitation, semi-supervised [35] and unsupervised [36] machine-learning

approaches have also been  utilized for anomaly detection to address the challenge of

unbalanced datasets.

  Machine learning (ML) has added value in acoustic-based process monitoring of LPBF by

identifying difficult patterns in complex data that are not possible by human interpretation.

However, it fails to provide valuable fundamental insight related to process dynamics, limiting

the broader adaptation of acoustic monitoring as a primary monitoring technique. In recent

research [37],  the acoustic signature produced by keyhole vapor depression is linked to the

whistle model used in aeroacoustics by using a non-dimensional Strouhal number. This

mechanistic understanding unfolds the complex phenomena of vapor dynamics and related

acoustic signatures. Researchers have also combined multiple sensors [17,38], in-situ, and ex-

situ [39] X-ray imaging to establish the correlation between AE footprints and physical events.

In a study [40], ex-situ radiography was used to identify the keyhole pore location and extract

a specific portion of the acoustic signal related to pore formation. The result indicated that

frequencies of 10-50 kHz were most important for detecting pores. Gorgannejad et al. [41]

presented a multimodal  data  fusion approach  for  the  detection  of keyhole pores by

simultaneously recording data using both coaxial and off-axis photodiodes and microphones.

In-situ high-speed synchrotron X-ray enabled monitoring of subsurface defect formation with

a temporal resolution of 50 𝜇𝑠. The study stated a strong correlation between keyhole pore

formation and  frequency  oscillation around 30-35 kHz and  highlighted  the  superior

performance of the microphone over the photodiode. In another study [7], synchronized use of

X-ray  imaging  and  acoustic  monitoring  captured  acoustic  footprints  of  inter-regime

instabilities provoked under constant process parameters, and a simple filtering algorithm wasproposed to predict the melting regime. In a similar experimental setup [42], a distinct acoustic

signature was captured for pore removal during remelting. This further emphasizes the unique

potential of acoustic monitoring for defect healing monitoring. Furthermore, the use of the

SBAE sensor was demonstrated to effectively capture martensitic phase transformation and

cracking in Ti64 [43].

  The increasing focus on acoustic monitoring reflects its potential in LPBF. However, limited

attention has been given to understanding the nature of acoustic signatures and their correlation

with actual physical changes in the processing condition. This paper aims to bridge this gap by

establishing a link between acoustic signatures and actual physical events by utilizing an air-

borne acoustic emission sensor and high-speed camera. A combination of high-frequency

microphone and a high sampling rate extracted important high-frequency information related

to process dynamics. The work focuses mainly on the influence of two process inherent

parameters: vector scan sequence direction, i.e, the direction in which the successive vectors

in one layer are moving, and the orientation of the scan vector with respect to the microphone.

The hatching pattern used in this study also links these two parameters, and they are always

perpendicular to each other. However, careful consideration was made with the experimental

design to investigate their individual effects. Variation of the acoustic signal signatures was

linked to a directionality of the emission source, which was corroborated by spatter ejection

trajectories  as observed by  high-speed camera. To  the  authors’ knowledge, no such

investigation has been reported in the literature.

  The current study thus highlights two important contextual variables: vector scan sequence

direction and scan vector direction for LPBF. The primary focus of this work is on establishing

the relationship between these contextual variables and the underlying physical phenomena.

However, in other manufacturing applications, studies have demonstrated the benefit of using

of context awareness in process monitoring [44–47]. Therefore, integrating this contextual

information could be beneficial for further improving the performance of machine learning

models.

2. Methodology

2.1. Machine and material

In this study, experiments were conducted using an in-house developed laser powder bed fusion

machine equipped with a 1 kW fiber laser with a wavelength of 1080 nm working in CW

(continuous wave) mode. The measured 1/𝑒2 spot diameter and the focal length of the systemare 37.5 𝜇𝑚 and 340 𝑚𝑚 respectively. The build chamber was filled with argon, and after

multiple inert cycles, 150 mbar overpressure was maintained during the printing. These inert

cycles result in extremely low oxygen content inside the chamber (below 50 ppm), preventing

oxidation during the process. Additionally, a constant crossflow was maintained over the

powder bed using a fan and a suction slit to remove fumes, spatters, and condensates produced

during melting. Argon gas was continuously recirculated through a filter throughout the

process.

      Commercially available gas-atomized SS316L powder, procured from Carpenter

Additive with particle size distribution ranging from 15- 53 𝜇𝑚 was used for the experiments.

The primary components and chemical composition of the powder are detailed in Table 1. Prior

to the experiments, the powder was dried in a vacuum oven to remove possible moisture

content for better flowability during recoating. In multiple experiments, a square cross-section

of 10 mm x 10 mm with varying height and a layer thickness of 30 μm was printed at the same

location at the center of the stainless steel base plate. The cross-section was scanned using a

Zig-Zag scanning strategy, with scan vectors aligned along the edges to maintain a consistent

vector length. The laser power, scan speed, and hatch distance applied during the experiments

were 190 W, 900 mm/s, and 80 𝜇𝑚 respectively. The process parameters were selected based

on pre-experimental trials, and the set resulting in a fully dense part (optimal parameter) was

chosen for this study.

Include columns: Parameter, Recommended Values, and Source. Cover rod diameter (0.8-3 mm), material (stainless steel, alumina), length (100-700 mm), thermal reduction capability, signal loss vs direct mounting (~10-13 dB for aluminum waveguide), concentrator tip types (exponential, conical, stepwise), dispersion (Pochhammer-Chree modes), and spring force. Include data from Zelenyak 2015, Zakharov 2010, Kazys 2021, and Jolly 1994."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Parameter | Recommended values / design implications | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Rod diameter | **0.8–3.0 mm** is the published practical range for informative AE transmission in rod/wire guides. A **1.59 mm** diameter was experimentally/model validated; increasing diameter raised the A0 amplitude, which approached saturation near **4.77 mm**, while 1.59 mm matched the sensor tip and preserved S0 response. | Zakharov et al. (2010); Zelenyak et al. (2015) (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) |
| Material | Prefer **stainless/carbon steel** for strength and weldability or **alumina** for electrical/thermal isolation. In an aluminium-plate model, steel and alumina had approximately **3.5 dB relative reduction**, brass about **5 dB**, and aluminium about **10 dB**; impedance matching and temperature-dependent properties must be considered. | Zelenyak et al. (2015); Kazys and Vaskeliene (2021) (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) |
| Length | Use the shortest length that keeps the sensor cool and separates early reflections: approximately **100–300 mm** for a 200 °C plate; up to **700 mm** for much hotter sources. Published examples include **145 mm**, **276–306 mm**, **600 mm**, and **700 mm**. Each additional **76.5 mm** produced about **15 µs** arrival delay in one model, but little change in the relative FFT spectrum. | Zelenyak et al. (2015); Kazys and Vaskeliene (2021) (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) |
| Thermal reduction capability | A **145 mm** tapered stainless-steel or titanium rod reduced a **200 °C tip to about 50 °C** at the transducer. A **700 mm SS304** wire/strip guide reduced a **600 °C tip to about 26 °C**. Thermal performance depends strongly on diameter, convection, clamping and heat sinking. | Kazys and Vaskeliene (2021) (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) |
| Signal loss versus direct mounting | A **1.59 mm × 306 mm aluminium** waveguide produced approximately **13 dB amplitude loss** relative to direct mounting. Material comparisons showed aluminium around **10 dB** reduction versus about **3.5 dB** for steel/alumina; these values are geometry- and mode-dependent rather than universal per-unit-length attenuation constants. | Zelenyak et al. (2015) (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009) |
| Hot-end tip/contact | Use a flat, polished tip normal to the plate for repeatable spring contact, or weld/braze the guide where permanence is acceptable. Published terminating concentrators include **stepwise, conical and exponential** profiles; the **exponential concentrator** was reported to minimize reflection and distortion when matching a thin rod to a larger sensor face. Hemispherical and inclined tips are specialized alternatives for focusing or mode conversion. | Zakharov et al. (2010); Kazys and Vaskeliene (2021) (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) |
| Dispersion and modes | Cylindrical rods support multiple **Pochhammer–Chree longitudinal, flexural and torsional modes**; group velocity varies with frequency–diameter product, broadening an impulsive AE waveform and biasing arrival-time location. Thin rods limit the number of modes but can reduce amplitude. Zelenyak’s plate/rod system was dominated by **A0**, with S0 also identifiable; rectangular strips can support a less-dispersive SH mode. Calibrate using the actual guide, band and temperature. | Zakharov et al. (2010); Zelenyak et al. (2015); Kazys and Vaskeliene (2021) (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011) |
| Spring/contact force | A published spring-loaded acoustic coupler used **2–5 lbf (9–22 N)** at the rod tip. Treat this as a starting range: use a Belleville or coil spring to maintain constant load through thermal cycling, then optimize force by pencil-lead-break transfer measurements while checking that the guide does not indent or constrain the plate. | Jolly (1994) (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038) |
| Practical starting design for a 200 °C LPBF plate | Start with a **1.5–2.0 mm diameter, 150–250 mm long 304/316 stainless-steel rod**, a polished flat hot tip, **10–20 N** spring preload, and a larger cool-end shoe/concentrator matched to the sensor. Expect roughly **5–15 dB** insertion loss and determine the actual 100–500 kHz transfer function after installation. | Engineering synthesis of the cited waveguide results (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000037) |


*Table: Published dimensions, materials, thermal isolation, insertion loss, modal behavior and contact loading for high-temperature AE waveguides. The final row translates the evidence into a practical starting design for a 200 °C LPBF build plate.*

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:

Use the tools to answer the question: Context: we are designing a lab-built desktop laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for small-batch screening of aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, 6061, 7075 and grain-refined variants with Zr, Sc or TiB2). Laser: 500 W single-mode CW fibre laser at 1070 nm (IPG YLR-500 class) into a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (marking speed up to about 1.1 m/s at f = 160 mm) and a Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta lens (f = 160 mm), giving a ~96 um 1/e2 spot diameter (48-75 um spots are options). Expected process window: 200-350 W, 0.4-1.1 m/s, 30 um layers, ~0.1 mm hatch. Build plates are 25, 50 or 75 mm across, heated to 200 C (500 C reserved). Chamber: ~280 x 190 x 120 mm inside, vacuum-purged then argon at +5 to +20 mbar, with an argon cross-flow of 2.5-3.3 m/s over the plate (140-200 L/min) from a slot nozzle on the back wall to an outlet slot at the front; a cover slide sits under a lid window ~130 mm above the plate.

We want acoustic emission (AE) monitoring of cracking during LPBF of crack-prone aluminium alloys (6061, 7075). The build plate (25-75 mm across, 6061) sits on graphite foil on a heater block (200 C, up to 500 C later) that stands on three Macor ceramic standoffs on a piston with a hollow rod; the piston slides in a bore sealed by an O-ring, and the module is swapped often.

1. AE in LPBF: which papers detected cracking (hot or cold) with structure-borne AE; sensor types and models, frequency bands, sampling rates, preamp gains and thresholds; how they told crack signals from recoater, gas-flow and pump noise. Any for Al alloys besides Seleznev et al. 2022?
2. Mounting through a heated, multi-interface stack: transmission loss across dry or bolted contacts, graphite foil and ceramic standoffs; typical dB loss per interface at 100-500 kHz; how contact pressure and couplants (high-temperature grease, gold or aluminium foil) change it.
3. Waveguides for high-temperature AE: rod diameter, material, length, tip and contact design, spring force, dispersion (Pochhammer-Chree modes) and attenuation at 100-500 kHz; published designs (welding, nuclear, LPBF heated plates) and how much signal they lose against direct mounting.
4. High-temperature AE sensors (MISTRAS/PAC D9215, Vallen VS-HT series, KRN and others): temperature ratings and sensitivities; whether a sensor can sit on a 200 C plate.
5. Calibration: Hsu-Nielsen pencil-lead breaks, path-loss measurement, and how often a removable plate's acoustic coupling should be re-checked.
6. Signal processing used to place cracks in time and layer: waveform features, clustering, machine learning; false-alarm rates where reported.

Give quantitative values and sources.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT Metal-based Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) suffers from a lack of repeatability and is challenging to model, making their quality monitoring essential and demanding. The reason lies in the high dynamics taking place during the interaction of the laser with metallic powders. To bring this technology to mass production, industries are only interested in the process regime where the built layer's quality meets their standards. All other process regimes leading to poor mechanical properties and/or defect formation such as balling, Lack of Fusion (LoF) pores, keyhole pores, delamination, and crack propagation irrespective of their different regimes are considered anomalies. Today, the common methodology for monitoring uses conventional/supervised Machine Learning (ML) algorithms for the classification task. However, it requires collecting a balanced dataset corresponding to each investigated regime from the sensors, which is very expensive and time-consuming. As an alternative, the article proposes a semi-supervised approach where the defect-free regime can be differentiated from the anomalies by familiarising the ML algorithms only with the distribution of acoustic signatures corresponding to the defect-free regime. This work presents two generative Convolutional Neural Network architectures based on Variational Auto-Encoder and General Adversarial Network. As a result, we could classify the anomaly regimes with 96 and 97% accuracy, respectively.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Powder Bed Fusion – Laser Based/Metal (PBF-LB/M), respective Laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) has become a key additive manufacturing method, driving the need for robust monitoring techniques to ensure process stability and reproducibility. In-situ monitoring methods are broadly categorized into optical and acoustic approaches, each with distinct advantages. Acoustic methods, unlike optical ones, can capture emissions from within the substrate and are often more cost-effective. Most PBF-LB/M monitoring systems rely on either airborne or structure-borne sensors, rarely on both.</jats:p>
               <jats:p>This work demonstrates a dual-sensor system integrating airborne and structure-borne sensors to leverage their complementary strengths for predicting both the process state of a PBF-LB/M-machine and defects (e.g. cracks or delamination, visible via secondary process emissions) occuring during the build. Using a fine-tuned neural network, both sensor types individually, as well as their combination, achieved a classification accuracy of ≈ 99 % for predicting the process state based on acquired emissions. Additionally, the structure-borne sensor proved superior in detection of secondary process emissions and slightly more accurate in process state classification. The compact form factor of the structure-borne sensor further enhances system flexibility, making this dual-sensor approach a versatile solution for PBF-LB/M monitoring.</jats:p>

Abstract:

Additive manufacturing (AM) metal parts offers opportunities for various industrial applications. From individual production of spare parts for unique mechanical components to prototyping of complex structures, the possibilities of production using the additive manufacturing process are manifold. One common AM technique is the Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB/M) process, where a laser is used to selectively melt metal powder and create the parts layer wise as designed in a model. During manufacturing certain defects like pores, cracks and lack of fusion may be created in the built parts. As AM parts often have complex geometries, a postprocess non-destructive testing is difficult or even not possible. Thus, different optical monitoring techniques are applied to detect flaws during the build process with the aim to detect and repair defects right away during the manufacturing process. However, optical monitoring system require a clear view of the melt pool and quite expensive equipment. Acoustic monitoring by AE sensors attached to the built plate would be a cheaper alternative which also can be used without visual contact to the building chamber. This paper shows a first approach of an AE based process monitoring. The build plate of a PBF-LB/M machine therefore was adapted to hold four AE sensors that are then used to monitor the process. The build process itself creates AE signals caused by the melting and cooling and the mechanical application of powder. The formation of pores and cracks is expected to create additional acoustic emissions that will be distinct from the AE pattern from the printing process. This AE signals can be linked to the different layers of the printed part or in the long run to the laser position. Results from the first tests in a customized LPBF machine will be shown as well as the implementation of AE into the PBF-LB/M machine.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a pivotal technology in component fabrication, renowned for its capabilities in freeform fabrication, material efficiency, and integrated design-to-manufacturing processes. As a critical branch of AM, metal additive manufacturing (MAM) has garnered significant attention for producing metal parts. However, process anomalies during MAM can pose safety risks, while internal defects in as-built parts detrimentally affect their service performance. These concerns underscore the necessity for robust in-process monitoring of both the MAM process and the quality of the resulting components. This review first delineates common MAM techniques and popular in-process monitoring methods. It then elaborates on the fundamental principles of acoustic emission (AE), including the configuration of AE systems and methods for extracting characteristic AE parameters. The core of the review synthesizes applications of AE technology in MAM, categorizing them into three key aspects: (1) hardware setup, which involves a comparative analysis of sensor selection, mounting strategies, and noise suppression techniques; (2) parametric characterization, which establishes correlations between AE features and process dynamics (e.g., process parameter deviations, spattering, melting/pool stability) as well as defect formation (e.g., porosity and cracking); and (3) intelligent monitoring, which focuses on the development of classification models and the integration of feedback control systems. By providing a systematic overview, this review aims to highlight the potential of AE as a powerful tool for real-time quality assurance in MAM.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In Wire and Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) and fusion welding, various defects such as porosity, cracks, deformation and lack of fusion can occur during the fabrication process. These have a strong impact on the mechanical properties and can also lead to failure of the manufactured parts during service. These defects can be recognized using non-destructive testing (NDT) methods so that the examined workpiece is not harmed. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of various NDT techniques for WAAM and fusion welding, including laser-ultrasonic, acoustic emission with an airborne optical microphone, optical emission spectroscopy, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy, laser opto-ultrasonic dual detection, thermography and also in-process defect detection via weld current monitoring with an oscilloscope. In addition, the novel research conducted, its operating principle and the equipment required to perform these techniques are presented. The minimum defect size that can be identified via NDT methods has been obtained from previous academic research or from tests carried out by companies. The use of these techniques in WAAM and fusion welding applications makes it possible to detect defects and to take a step towards the production of high-quality final components.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) is an arc-welding-based Additive Manufacturing (AM) process that enables the cost-effective production of large metallic components. Despite its potential, industrial deployment remains limited due to process instabilities and defect formation arising from the complex thermoelectric and metallurgical phenomena inherent to layer-by-layer deposition. Reliable online monitoring is therefore essential to ensure process consistency and part quality. This study proposes an acoustic emission (AE)-based monitoring strategy as a robust, noise-resilient alternative to microphone-based sensing, combined with an unsupervised deep learning approach to address the limitations of state-of-the-art supervised methods. The influence of sensor placement is experimentally assessed to identify an industrially viable configuration without sacrificing detection capability. Based on this analysis, a novel placement strategy is proposed. To investigate the performance of AE-based monitoring, conventional control charts and tree-based anomaly detection methods are compared with a novel approach that leverages automatic feature extraction from high-frequency acoustic emission data with a deep convolutional autoencoder (CAE). The proposed framework integrates tree-based anomaly detection with an additional clustering-based stage, enabling semi-supervised soft classification of anomaly severity. The results demonstrate that conventional control charts fail to detect subtle anomalies, whereas the use of frequency-domain energy instead of time-domain energy leads to a marked improvement in F2-score, increasing from 12% to 49%. The adoption of a convolutional autoencoder for automatic feature extraction further enhances Isolation Forest performance, raising the F2-score from 62.9% (obtained with manual feature extraction) to 77%. Moreover, it is shown that when unlabelled data are available and anomalies represent only a small fraction of the dataset, as in this case study (where they account for approximately 8%), the proposed clustering-based approach enables the stratification of anomaly severity, thereby providing a soft decision-support mechanism for prognostics.</jats:p>

Abstract:
During the last decades, structural health monitoring (SHM) systems are used in order to detect damage in structures. We have developed a novel structural health monitoring approach, the so-called “effective structural health monitoring” (eSHM) system. The current SHM system is incorporated into a metallic structure by means of additive manufacturing (AM) and has the possibility to advance life safety and reduce direct operative costs. It operates based on a network of capillaries that are integrated into an AM structure. The internal pressure of the capillaries is continuously monitored by a pressure sensor. When a crack nucleates and reaches the capillary, the internal pressure changes signifying the existence of the flaw. The main objective of this paper is to evaluate the crack detection capacity of the eSHM system and crack location accuracy by means of various non-destructive testing (NDT) techniques. During this study, detailed acoustic emission (AE) analysis was applied in AM materials for the first time in order to investigate if phenomena like the Kaiser effect and waveform parameters used in conventional metals can offer valuable insight into the damage accumulation of the AM structure as well. Liquid penetrant inspection, eddy current and radiography were also used in order to confirm the fatigue damage and indicate the damage location on un-notched four-point bending AM metallic specimens with an integrated eSHM system. It is shown that the eSHM system in combination with NDT can provide correct information on the damage condition of additive manufactured metals.

Abstract:
Large format additive manufacturing (LFAM) proved to have a great potential to become an adjacent technology to traditional manufacturing methods. One of the sectors LFAM is targeting is rapid tool/mold development for composites. This includes large mold structures used for high-temperature molding techniques (in-oven or autoclave). Although, these large printed structures (reaching hundreds of pounds) develop thermal-residual stress during cool-down and can eventually crack, turning the structure into waste. Acoustic emission (AE), a passive non-intrusive global nondestructive evaluation (NDE) technique, was used to monitor crack growth and can provide the right tools that can be used for feedback loop for corrective action. This research performs thermal testing on a large AM mold with preexisting cracks, in an attempt to monitor crack growth using AE. AE was able to detect, identify and locate the crack source by means of acoustic features, waveform characteristics, spectrum analysis, and difference in arrival times.

Abstract:
Acoustic emission (AE) testing is a widely used nondestructive testing (NDT) method to investigate material failure. When environmental conditions are harmful for the operation of the sensors, waveguides are typically mounted in between the inspected structure and the sensor. Such waveguides can be built from different materials or have different designs in accordance with the experimental needs. All these variations can cause changes in the acoustic emission signals in terms of modal conversion, additional attenuation or shift in frequency content. A finite element method (FEM) was used to model acoustic emission signal propagation in an aluminum plate with an attached waveguide and was validated against experimental data. The geometry of the waveguide is systematically changed by varying the radius and height to investigate the influence on the detected signals. Different waveguide materials were implemented and change of material properties as function of temperature were taken into account. Development of the option of modeling different waveguide options replaces the time consuming and expensive trial and error alternative of experiments. Thus, the aim of this research has important implications for those who use waveguides for AE testing.

<jats:p>Acoustic emission (AE) technology has been extensively applied in the damage assessment of steel strands; however, it remains inadequate in identifying and quantifying the number of strand fractures, which limits the accuracy and reliability of prestressed structure monitoring. In this study, a test platform based on practical engineering was built. The AE monitoring method using a waveguide rod was applied to identify signals from different numbers of strand fractures, and their acoustic characteristics were analyzed using Fourier transform and multi-bandwidth wavelet transform. The propagation attenuation behavior of the AE signals in the waveguide rod was then analyzed, and the optimal parameters for field monitoring as well as the maximum number of plates suitable for series beam plates were determined. The results show that AE signals decrease exponentially with an increasing propagation distance, and attenuation models for various AE parameters were established. As the number of strand fractures increases, the amplitude of the dominant frequency increases significantly, and the energy distribution shifts towards higher-frequency bands. This finding introduces a novel approach for quantifying fractures in steel strands, enhancing the effectiveness of AE technology in monitoring and laying a foundation for the development of related technologies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This article presents a very precise approach to measuring temperature in a wide temperature range using ultrasonic waves. A lead zirconate titanate (PZT) piezoelectric transducer is used to excite ultrasonic shear waves and a solid stainless steel waveguide is selected to confine the ultrasonic wave propagation path. The shape and dimensions of the waveguide were theoretically optimized and numerically simulated to propagate robust, non-dispersive wave, and protect the fragile PZT from high temperature. Ultrasonic wave velocity is highly temperature dependent. The travelling time of wavepacket along the waveguide exhibits a corresponding relationship with the average temperature at measurement zone of the waveguide. Detailed experimental verification and validation processes, together with a calibration stage, were conducted up to 200°C, a temperature that is on par with the operating range of the resistance temperature detector (RTD) used for calibration. Stability test demonstrated that our technique attains a high accuracy (i.e. ±0.1%) which is comparable with the highest precision standard of commercial RTDs along the calibrated temperature range. Temperature tracking test was operated to unfold the temperature measuring and tracking capability of the ultrasonic wave technique in different liquids. This ultrasonic technique is robust and customizable, hence providing a promising alternative for accurate and stable contact thermometry.

Abstract:
The acoustic impedance mismatch between transducer materials and medium in ultrasonic power transfer systems narrows the transduction bandwidth and causes losses through the back reflection of progressive pressure waves at the boundary between the transducers and medium. Capturing both resonances and losses due to impedance mismatch of interwoven elements is essential for advancing the development of these systems. We present a unified approach, based on the multiplication of a sequence of transfer matrices, to determine an equivalent acoustic impedance. The analytical model couples the properties of the transmitter and receiver with multiple matching layers and a single classical quarter-wave layer in controlled setups with the objective of minimizing reflections through acoustic impedance mismatch alleviation. Losses due to ultrasonic attenuation in the material layers and medium are also considered. The acoustic field at the receiver location constitutes the input to the coupled electro-elastic equations of the fluid-loaded and electrically-loaded piezoelectric receiver. Experiments are performed to identify the input acoustic pressure from a cylindrical transmitter to a receiver disk operating in the 33-mode of piezoelectricity. The results show significant enhancements in terms of the receiver’s electrical power output when implementing a two-layer matching structure. We present the results showing non-dimensional wave number variations versus characteristic impedance, which can be used to calculate the materials’ thicknesses for acoustically matching ultrasonic power transfer systems to an acoustic medium of interest at any desired resonant frequency while considering any type of glue or epoxy as the bonding layer. The derived physical models facilitate the development of high-fidelity matched systems with enhanced contactless power transmission.

Abstract:
An air-coupled ultrasonic technology is introduced as a new tool for evaluating the interfacial quality of bonded structures in this paper. Thus, a mathematical model including the stiffness coefficient, the transmission coefficient and the frequency, etc. is proposed. Two type resonant frequencies, namely, the first type resonance frequency (RFI) and the second type resonance frequency (RFII), have been obtained by numerical solving the model. The interval of the RFI is related to the thickness of a polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) layer. Similarly, the interval of the RFII depends on the thickness of an aluminum (Al) layer. In addition, the stiffness coefficient is associated with the RFI but not with the RFII. The RFI drifts to high-frequency with different speed from the low stiffness coefficient to the high stiffness coefficient, which no longer changes when the stiffness coefficient tends to infinity. The before-RFII moves faster than after-RFI in a “Period” of the RFII. With the increase of the stiffness coefficient, the transmission coefficient gradually increases, and then increases slowly when the stiffness coefficient approaches to a critical value. Several double-layer bonded samples with the different thicknesses were made to carry out air-coupled ultrasonic experiment. The change of stiffness coefficients was simulated by different bonding time. Transmission signals from ultrasonic testing were recorded for further processing. Comparing the experimental and simulation results, the stiffness coefficient of the bonded structure can be judged by the RFI and the transmission coefficient.

Piezoelectronics, as an efficient approach for energy conversion and sensing, have a far-reaching influence on energy harvesting, precise instruments, sensing, health monitoring and so on. A majority of the previous works on piezoelectronics concentrated on the materials that are applied at close to room temperatures. However, there is inadequate research on the materials for high-temperature piezoelectric applications, yet they also have important applications in the critical equipment of aeroengines and nuclear reactors in harsh and high-temperature conditions. In this review, we briefly introduce fundamental knowledge about the piezoelectric effect, and emphatically elucidate high-temperature piezoelectrics, involving: the typical piezoelectric materials operated in high temperatures, and the applications, limiting factors, prospects and challenges of piezoelectricity at high temperatures.

Abstract:
Piezoelectric sensing is of increasing interest for high-temperature applications in aerospace, automotive, power plants and material processing due to its low cost, compact sensor size and simple signal conditioning, in comparison with other high-temperature sensing techniques. This paper presented an overview of high-temperature piezoelectric sensing techniques. Firstly, different types of high-temperature piezoelectric single crystals, electrode materials, and their pros and cons are discussed. Secondly, recent work on high-temperature piezoelectric sensors including accelerometer, surface acoustic wave sensor, ultrasound transducer, acoustic emission sensor, gas sensor, and pressure sensor for temperatures up to 1,250 °C were reviewed. Finally, discussions of existing challenges and future work for high-temperature piezoelectric sensing are presented.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Développement de capteurs ultrasonores pour l’extension des mesures acoustiques aux hautes températures dans les réacteurs expérimentaux</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">Ce travail de thèse porte sur l’étude et la réalisation d'une nouvelle génération de capteurs ultrasonore dédiés à la caractérisation des gaz de fission. Plus généralement, ces études concernent le développement de l’instrumentation du réacteur d’essai des matériaux Jules Horowitz (RJH), visant entre autre à effectuer le contrôle in situ de la composition du gaz libéré afin d’optimiser la durée de vie du combustible et le taux de combustion. La température de fonctionnement de ce nouveau réacteur devant se situer dans la plage entre 200 °C à 400 °C, la principale problématique concerne donc le développement d’un matériau piézoélectrique, capable de fonctionner dans la plage de température requise, et son intégration à un dispositif de détection.Nous proposons l’utilisation du sodium titanate de bismuth (NBT) développé par la méthode de la sérigraphie. Dans le but d'optimiser les conditions de fabrication des matériaux, plusieurs versions de matériaux piézoélectriques ont été produites au cours de cette thèse. Chacun des matériaux a été caractérisé (paramètres morphologiques, chimiques, électriques, diélectriques, piézoélectriques et électromécaniques) et des tests en fonction de la température ont été conduits. Après avoir démontré une bonne répétabilité dans la production du matériau, le protocole de fabrication des capteurs a été déterminé et un prototype de capteur ultrasonore a été réalisé.Ces capteurs ont été fabriqués par dépôt du matériau actif sur un substrat d'alumine. Après caractérisation des propriétés des capteurs, des essais ont montré une sensibilité acoustique importante à température ambiante. De plus, la possibilité d'une détection de gaz sur une gamme de pression de 50 à 70 bars a été démontrée par l'intégration d’un capteur dans une enceinte. Pour vérifier la possibilité d'application du capteur à la détection de gaz dans des environnements hostiles (haute température), un modèle théorique basé sur les propriétés électromécaniques et les équations d’adaptation d’impédance a été introduit. Il a été démontré théoriquement que le capteur est capable d'effectuer des mesures de gaz de la température ambiante jusqu’à 350 °C.</jats:p>
