Abstract:
This paper presents the results from conducting a series of experiments with a Hsu-Nielsen Source, accompanied by corresponding numerical simulations on a solid block. The aim being to illustrate a Finite Element Analysis (FEA) approach for simulating Acoustic Emission (AE) wave propagation in a Hsu-Nielsen Source, by employing virtual sensors to enhance existing AE research methodologies. The objective was to examine and establish the actual unload rate derived from Pencil Lead Breaks (PLBs) by comparing results from simulations and experimental trials. These experiments and simulations were conducted using a solid cylindrical steel block, capturing the propagating Acoustic AE waves from both sources over a two-second span. When comparing the experimental data with the simulation results, it is evident that replicating the structure of an impulsive AE source is feasible for brief durations. Furthermore, both the experimental and simulated signals on the steel cylinder displayed comparable patterns in the initial 25-30 µs. The methodology presented in this study demonstrates the effectiveness of Finite Element Analysis (FEA) in precisely identifying the specific modes present in AE wave propagation, including the actual unload rates affecting the AE signals recorded.

Abstract:
Abstract: Acoustic Emission (AE) testing is a non-destructive evaluation technique that has gained significant attention in pipeline monitoring. Pencil-lead breaks (PLBs) are commonly used in reproducing and characterising sensors used in AE applications and have emerged as a valuable tool for calibration processes. This technique involves breaking a pencil lead by pressing it on the surface of the test structure and applying a bending moment at a given angle on a surface. The applied force produces a local deformation on the test surface, which is released when the lead breaks. The fracture in these PLBs is assumed to be a step unload; however, this is not the case. In this work, a series of PLB source experiments complemented with parallel numerical simulations were carried out to investigate the actual unload rate by correlating the relationship between AE speed, frequency, and power from PLBs. This was achieved by varying the simulation unload rates recorded over a duration of 2 s on a steel pipe and comparing to the experiment. Analysis of the investigated results from the experimental and numerical models suggests that although the AE line structure of a PLB can be reproduced by simulation for short times only (1 µs), the actual unload rate for PLBs is in the region of 10–8 s. It is concluded that FEA has the potential to help in the recovery of the temporal structure from real AE structures. The establishment of this model will provide a theoretical basis for future studies on the monitoring of non-impulsive AE sources such as impact on pipelines using finite element analysis.

Abstract:
<jats:p>A reliable numerical reproduction of acoustic emission (AE) tests requires a clear understanding of simulating the AE process. Here, we perform a comparative study of Pencil-Lead Break (PLB) tests on polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) plates using two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) finite element models, with emphasis on how the propagation medium is represented. A Hsu–Nielsen source is applied at the plate center, and responses are recorded at multiple locations along the plate symmetry axis. Sensors are modeled as perfect-contact sensors, neglecting the sensor effect. Thus, a 2D model with an axisymmetry assumption can be established only to reproduce the direct-wave response. While 2D modeling greatly reduces computational cost, particularly for large plates whose in-plane dimensions far exceed thickness, noticeable discrepancies arise between 2D- and 3D-simulated signals. The direct waveforms are highly consistent, but differences appear after the direct-wave arrival. To clarify the origin of these discrepancies, we investigate the influences of plate size and geometry, mesh configuration, and sensor–source distance. In addition, we evaluate commonly used AE features to identify conditions under which 2D simulations remain valid. These findings provide practical guidance on the limitations and appropriate use of 2D models for interpreting PLB-based AE responses.</jats:p>

Abstract:

After 51 years continuously involved in acoustic emission (AE) testing and research, it has been interesting to look back over five decades. The equipment available in the early 1970s was primitive compared to now. At the start of that decade, only one, recently established, commercial company sold AE measurement equipment, and other useful equipment was internally built or adapted from other technologies. Further, the data that came from an AE monitored test was simply the number (counts) of penetrations of a fixed one-volt threshold expressed as an increasing total or a rate and recorded on an x-y plotter. The purpose of this “glimpse” is to present advances both within the author’s research as well as those that were adopted from others research that were viewed as moving AE technology forward. This “glimpse” is not intended to be comprehensive, instead it is limited to aspects the author was involved in. Among the topics to be covered are advances such as understanding hydraulic test machine continuous noise, true rootmean-square (RMS) voltage measurements, inclusion particle fracture or decohesion, tension versus compression testing for unflawed metal samples, the pencil lead break, an acoustic emission signal simulator, broadband sensors, digital waveform recorders, large transversedimensioned plates, absolutely calibrated flat-with-frequency AE sensors, finite element modeling (FEM) in isotropic materials, validation of FEM, computer-based digital AE systems, intensity of frequency versus time of AE signals, superposition of group velocity results and FEM beyond the case of dipoles in an isotropic plate.

Abstract:

Acoustic emission testing is used to monitor the structural health by recording and analyzing sound signals 
originating from within a structure. Usually, sensors are attached at key positions on a structure under test to record 
and analyze these acoustic signals. For reliable measurements, the coupling of these sensors has to be assessed. 
For this purpose, artificial sound sources are commonly used which induce signals in the form of elastic waves 
into a structure allowing to approximately assess the frequency response function of the sensor coupling. To assess 
the coupling of sensors reliably by means of an artificial sound source, it has to exhibit high repeatability, i.e. small 
relative standard deviation (RSTD) with respect to some characteristic of interest. In this work, the repeatability 
of the pencil lead break, ball impact and an electromagnetic body-noise actuator is assessed across several 
repetitions. Through controlled and repeated excitation of the respective artificial sound sources on a concrete 
girder, the RSTD of the magnitude spectra of the artificial sound sources across frequency is assessed in the 
frequency range of about 0 kHz to 650 kHz. The ball impact and the actuator exhibited a RSTD of below 5 % of 
their magnitude spectra for frequencies below about 20 kHz, the maximum frequency for the actuator, whereas for 
the pencil lead break a RSTD of above 11 % was observed across the entire frequency range. An increase of the 
RSTD with increasing frequency was observed for the ball impact and the pencil lead break. The repeatability of 
the pencil lead break, for which a RSTD between 15 % to 40 % was observed for a broad frequency range of its 
amplitude spectrum, usually achieved a lower relative standard deviation than the ball impacts with 4 mm and 5 
mm balls above a frequency of about 60 kHz. A significant increase of the relative standard deviation for the 4 
mm and 5 mm ball was observed starting at about 20 kHz. Above about 60 kHz, the relative standard deviation of 
the 5 mm ball impact had risen to 30 % and more oscillating between about 30 - 50 %. At 200 kHz and more all 
signals were attenuated to background noise level by the concrete girder. It is concluded, that the pencil lead break 
is inferior with respect to repeatability below 40 kHz compared to the 4 mm and 5 mm ball impact and 
electromagnetic body-noise actuator, but performs equally well or better above 60 kHz. The repeatability of the 
investigated artificial sound sources depends on the investigated frequency range with no unique best. The most 
important finding is the increasing relative standard deviation of the ball impact with increasing frequency. As a 
result, the repeatability of the ball impact is questionable and should be investigated before using it in high 
precision experiments.

Abstract:
To calculate sound wave velocity, we performed the Hsu-Nielsen lead break experiment using the ANSYS/LS-DYNA finite element software. First, we identified the key problems in the finite element analysis, such as selecting the exciting force, dividing the grid density, and setting the calculation steps. Second, we established the finite element model of the sound wave transmission in a plate under the lead break simulation. Results revealed not only the transmission characteristics of the sound wave but also the simulation and calculation of the transmission velocity of the longitudinal and transverse waves through the time travel curve of the vibration velocity of the sound wave at various nodes. Finally, the Hsu-Nielsen lead break experiment was implemented. The results of the theoretical calculation and simulation analysis were consistent with the experimental results, thus demonstrating that the research method using the ANSYS/LS-DYNA software to simulate sound wave transmissions in acoustic emission experiments is feasible and effective.

Abstract:
There are many fields such as online monitoring of manufacturing processes, non-destructive testing in nuclear plants, or corrosion rate monitoring techniques of steel pipes in which measurements must be performed at elevated temperatures. For that high temperature ultrasonic transducers are necessary. In the presented paper, a literature review on the main types of such transducers, piezoelectric materials, backings, and the bonding techniques of transducers elements suitable for high temperatures, is presented. In this review, the main focus is on ultrasonic transducers with piezoelectric elements suitable for operation at temperatures higher than of the most commercially available transducers, i.e., 150 °C. The main types of the ultrasonic transducers that are discussed are the transducers with thin protectors, which may serve as matching layers, transducers with high temperature delay lines, wedges, and waveguide type transducers. The piezoelectric materials suitable for high temperature applications such as aluminum nitride, lithium niobate, gallium orthophosphate, bismuth titanate, oxyborate crystals, lead metaniobate, and other piezoceramics are analyzed. Bonding techniques used for joining of the transducer elements such as joining with glue, soldering, brazing, dry contact, and diffusion bonding are discussed. Special attention is paid to efficient diffusion and thermo-sonic diffusion bonding techniques. Various types of backings necessary for improving a bandwidth and to obtain a short pulse response are described.

Abstract:
Objective: Ultrasonic acoustic power transfer is an efficient mechanism for coupling energy to millimeter and sub-millimeter implants in the body. To date, published ultrasonically powered implants have been encapsulated with thin film polymers that are susceptible to well-documented failure modes in vivo, including water penetration and attack by the body. As with all medical implants, packaging with ceramic or metallic materials can reduce water vapor transmission and improve biostability to provide decadal device lifetime. In this paper, we evaluate methods of coupling ultrasonic energy to the interior of ceramic packages. Methods: The classic wave approach and modal expansion are used to obtain analytical expressions for ultrasonic transmission through two different package designs and these approaches are validated experimentally. A candidate package design is demonstrated using alumina packages and titanium lids, designed to be acoustically transparent at ultrasonic frequencies. Results: Bulk modes are shown to be more effective at coupling ultrasonic energy to a piezoelectric receiver than flexural modes. Using bulk modes, packaged motes have an overall link efficiency of roughly 10%, compared to 25% for unpackaged motes. Packaging does not have a significant effect on translational misalignment penalties, but does increase angular misalignment penalties. Passive amplitude-modulated backscatter communication is demonstrated. Conclusion: Thin lids enable the use of ultrasonically coupled devices even with package materials of very different acoustic impedance. Significance: This work provides an analysis and method for designing packages that enable ultrasonic coupling with implantable medical devices, which could facilitate clinical translation.

For LPBF crack detection, the authors used a Physical Acoustics PCI-2-based acoustic-emission system with a broadband high-temperature D9215 AE sensor coupled directly to the underside of the build plate using Molykote 41 grease. The signal was amplified by 40 dB using a low-noise preamplifier, filtered with a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter, and digitized by an 18-bit PCI-2 board at 2 MHz. Events were recorded when their amplitude exceeded an individually selected threshold of approximately 90–100 dB; the threshold was adjusted before each build to sit just above the measured background-noise amplitude. Monitoring continued throughout additive manufacturing and for two hours afterward to capture cracking during cooling. To assess interference, baseline signals were collected before processing while operating machine functions separately, including power, gas/powder rake movement, and pump on/off states. The excerpt states that machine modules did not significantly influence the AE signal, with the exception of the inert-gas circulation pump, whose noise amplitude was reportedly much higher (the displayed excerpt begins the comparison as 2 V versus 0.2 V). Thus, recoater/rake and other machine noise were evaluated experimentally and found insignificant, while pump activity was the principal identified noise source; the excerpt does not provide the complete method for separating pump noise from crack events.

Abstract:
Despite the significant advances made involving the additive manufacturing (AM) of metals, including those related to both materials and processes, challenges remain in regard to the rapid qualification and insertion of such materials into applications. In general, understanding the process–microstructure–property interrelationships is essential. To successfully understand these interrelationships on a process-by-process basis and exploit such knowledge in practice, leveraging monitoring, modeling, and statistical analysis is necessary. Monitoring allows for the identification and measurement of parameters and features associated with important physical processes that may vary spatially and temporally during the AM processes that will influence part properties, including spatial variations within a single part and part-to-part variability, and, ultimately, quality. Modeling allows for the prediction of physical processes, material states, and properties of future builds by creating material state abstractions that can then be tested or evolved virtually. Statistical analysis permits the data from monitoring to inform modeling, and vice versa, under the added consideration that physical measurements and mathematical abstractions contain uncertainties. Throughout this review, the feedstock, energy source, melt pool, defects, compositional distribution, microstructure, texture, residual stresses, and mechanical properties are examined from the points of view of monitoring, modeling, and statistical analysis. As with most active research subjects, there remain both possibilities and limitations, and these will be considered and discussed as appropriate.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT In additive manufacturing of metals, numerous techniques have been employed to sense print defects. Among these, acoustic-based sensing has the advantage of low cost and shows the most potential to identify both external and internal defects as an in-situ monitoring system. Using acoustic signals, researchers have broadly investigated non-machine learning and machine learning-based approaches to identify defects like balling, micro defects, lack of fusion pores, keyhole pores, cracks, and porosity. While most of these works have shown promising results for laser-based AM systems, few have explored how acoustic signals can be used effectively for Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) defect detection. This paper proposes a methodology to construct machine learning (ML)-based models on identifying geometrically defective bead segments using acoustic signals during the WAAM process. Geometrically defective bead segment or geometric defect is a defect that causes voids in the final printed part due to incomplete fusion between two non-uniform overlapping bead segments. Such a defect is currently not explored in the literature. The proposed methodology uses a novel dataset labeling approach to identify good and bad bead segments based on an optimal threshold of the range of mean curvature. Furthermore, the methodology targets defective bead segments based on acoustic feature inputs like Principal Components (PC) or Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC). To understand the resulting performance of the defect identification models constructed based on the proposed methodology, experiments are performed and tested on a variety of ML models (KNN, SVM, RF, NN, and CNN) based on the Inconel 718 material. The results show that the combinatorics of two acoustic input features and five ML models can be able to identify geometrically defective segments accurately with F1 score that ranges from 80% to 85%.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal additive manufacturing (AM) facilitates the production of geometrically complex components, yet its broader industrial use remains limited by the risk of defect formation and uncertainties in their detection, originating from the highly dynamic and high-temperature process environment. To make additive manufacturing more reliable and establish high-quality parts, it is important to understand how these defects form and how their characteristics appear during the process. This review explains the main causes of common defects, such as cracking, porosity, lack of fusion, and inclusions in metal AM processes, including Powder Bed Fusion and Directed Energy Deposition. It also connects main defect formation mechanisms to the optical, thermal, acoustic, and spectroscopic signals that can be measured during the process. Moreover, it is described how commonly used in situ monitoring systems work and how their signals correspond to melt pool dynamics, vapor plume, particle movement, and the solidification process for each kind of defect. An overview is provided of how data from these systems are analyzed, including the extraction of features from images, the evaluation of temperature fields, and the use of time and frequency domain techniques for various signals. By linking the physics of defect formation to measurable process signals, the interpretation of sensor data is enabled, and potential strategies for monitoring specific problems are outlined. Finally, recent developments are examined, including the integration of multiple sensors, advanced feature-representation approaches, and real-time data interpretation coupled with adaptive control. Together, these directions represent promising advances towards more intelligent and reliable monitoring systems for the future of metal AM.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>The demand for metal alloys that can perform at extreme temperatures above 1100 °C while remaining manufacturable has sparked renewed interest in printable oxide dispersion strengthened (ODS) alloys. Recently, NASA developed an ODS alloy designed for additive manufacturing, known as GRX-810, which has demonstrated exceptional tensile and creep performance at temperatures of 1093 °C and higher. In the present study, tensile tests of GRX-810 are conducted up to 1316 °C and creep tests are performed in both the horizontal and vertical orientations, relative to the build direction. Thermal cycling is executed at 1100 °C, 1200 °C, and 1300 °C in air. The oxidation behavior of GRX-810 is compared to that of alumina forming single crystal Ni-base superalloys and chromia-forming wrought alloys such as superalloys 718 and 625. High resolution atomic-scale characterization and atomistic modeling are employed to explain the exceptional high temperature properties observed in GRX-810, particularly in relation to the unique, finer trigonal yttrium oxides produced during the additive manufacturing process.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this paper, the guided ultrasonic wave propagation characteristics in the axisymmetric pre-stressed viscoelastic waveguide for acoustic emission (AE) monitoring, using the semi-analytical finite element (SAFE) method, is studied broadly. For the numerical investigation, a single high-strength steel wire is considered. A comprehensive and in-depth study on the AE signal’s propagation characteristics is carried out based on the SAFE method. Both undamped and damped waveguides are considered for attaining SAFE solutions and presented in a detailed manner. The SAFE method for an axisymmetric cross-section in cylindrical coordinates analyzes the two main influencing factors of steel wire in a practical scenario: Material damping and initial tension. For the effect of initial stress, the calculation shows that the initial tensile stress can increase and decrease the energy velocity and attenuation factor of most modal waves above the cut-off frequency, and the effect is linear. Some longitudinal wave modes in the high-frequency region show their potential for AE monitoring as these modes have a low attenuation factor and small external surface vibration. By considering various states of initial stress in a damped waveguide, the effect of pre-stress on the dispersion characteristics is understood in a better manner. A non-destructive testing (NDT) mechanism for pre-stressed steel wire using AE monitoring is proposed for the health monitoring of structures.

Abstract:
The problem of seismic activity and carrying out anti-seismic measures is extremely urgent at the present time. A large number of regions are more or less earthquake-prone and sometimes new regions, in which seismic activity has not been recorded before, fall into this category. Various methods of seismic load reduction are used to build new structures and support existing structures in these areas. The seismic load is transmitted to the structure through the foundation, therefore one of the effective ways to reduce it is to change the properties of the foundation. If instead of soil, which perfectly transmits impulses of seismic load, fill in a certain order with material that dampens these impulses - the desired effect can be achieved. The article analyzes the way of how one-dimensional pulse becomes attenuated in a multilayer rod. The layers in the rod are arranged in a periodical order and have contrasting acoustic properties. Numerical analysis is carried out using the finite element method. A pulse hitting the interface between the media undergoes multiple reflection and refraction, which causes damping in a purely mechanical system. The analysis shows that the larger the difference in acoustic properties between adjacent layers, the higher the attenuation of acoustical properties becomes.

Abstract:
The speed of sound waves in rods depends on the relationship between wavelength and rod dimensions. It differs from the speeds readily available in tables, and from what is often learned during most introductory courses on solid-state physics. Metallic rods with diameters in the centimetre range excited with sound waves of tens of kHz will behave as dispersive media. Here, the speed of sound in metallic titanium rods of different lengths is measured using two different methodologies: (1) from the time of flight and (2) from the wavelength and frequency of standing waves that form in the rod. The latter allows analyzing the results in light of Pochhammer-Cree dispersion. The reflection coefficient is also determined both from time and from frequency response. Two off-the-shelf piezoelectric transducers, a function generator, an oscilloscope, and a lock-in amplifier were used. We have used a low-frequency square wave (of tens of Hz) in the first case and a sine wave with frequencies that range from audible to ultrasound in the second case. Experimental results show that the speed of sound decreases as the wavelength decreases. The Pochhammer-Chree dispersion equation was numerically solved to fit the experimental data that can be used to estimate both the Young modulus and the Poisson ratio. A practical empirical formula that allows data analysis without explicitly solving the Pochhammer-Chree equation is suggested.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Acoustic Emission (AE) and Guided Ultrasonic Waves (GUWs) are non-destructive testing (NDT) methods in several industrial sectors for, e.g., proof testing and periodic inspection of pressure vessels, storage tanks, pipes or pipelines and leak or corrosion detection. AE and GUW also show potential for long-term Structural Health and Condition Monitoring (SHM and CM). With increasing computational power, even online monitoring of industrial manufacturing processes has become feasible. Combined with Artificial Intelligence (AI) for analysis this may soon allow for efficient, automated online process control. AI also plays a role in predictive maintenance and cost optimization. Long-term SHM, CM and process control require sensor integration together with data acquisition equipment and possibly data analysis. This paper presents and discusses selected aspects of the long-term durability of sensor behavior, sensor coupling and measurement hardware and software. The aim is to identify research and development needs for reliable, cost-effective, long-term SHM and CM with AE and GUW under combined mechanical and environmental service loads.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Acoustic coupling agents serve as critical interfacial materials connecting piezoelectric transducers with microfluidic chips in acoustofluidic systems. Their performance directly impacts acoustic wave transmission efficiency, device reusability, and reliability in biomedical applications. Considering the rapidly growing body of research in the field of acoustic microfluidics, this review aims to serve as an all-in-one reference on the role of acoustic coupling agents and relevant considerations pertinent to acoustofluidic devices for anyone working in or seeking to enter the field of disposable acoustofluidic devices. To this end, this review seeks to summarize and categorize key aspects of acoustic couplants in the implementation of acoustofluidic devices by examining their underlying physical mechanisms, material classifications, and core applications of coupling agents in acoustofluidics. Gel-based coupling agents are particularly favored for their long-term stability, high coupling efficiency, and ease of preparation, making them integral to acoustic flow control applications. In practice, coupling agents facilitate microparticle trapping, droplet manipulation, and biosample sorting through acoustic impedance matching and wave mode conversion (e.g., Rayleigh-to-Lamb waves). Their thickness and acoustic properties (sound velocity, attenuation coefficient) further modulate sound field distribution to optimize acoustic radiation forces and thermal effects. However, challenges remain regarding stability (evaporation, thermal degradation) and chip compatibility. Further aspects of research into gel-based agents requiring attention include multilayer coupled designs, dynamic thickness control, and enhancing biocompatibility to advance acoustofluidic technologies in point-of-care diagnostics and high-throughput analysis.

Abstract:
A multi-physical signal correlation analysis method is proposed to identify the different tribological properties of materials. The acoustic emission (AE), contact resistance, and frictional force behaviors during dry sliding between four metals, 45# carbon steel, YG12 carbide, 2A12 aluminum alloy, and H62 brass, have been studied. Both positive and negative correlations between the root mean square of the amplified AE (AE RMS) signal and the frictional coefficient have been found in the experiments. In addition, the AE RMS signal and the contact resistance changed with changing sliding speed and normal load in different ways. The different correlation behaviors have been attributed to diverse tribological states under different experimental conditions due to different material characteristics. The correlation analysis provides a new method of quantitatively identifying the tribological states and the AE sources during frictional interaction. The observed anomalous correlations between the AE signal and frictional coefficient should be properly considered according to the different material properties during industrial friction condition monitoring using AE technology.

Abstract:
Over the last decade, acoustic methods, including acoustic emission (AE) and ultrasonic testing (UT), have been increasingly deployed for process diagnostics and health monitoring of electrochemical power devices, including batteries, fuel cells, and water electrolysers. These techniques are non-invasive, highly sensitive, and low-cost, providing a high level of spatial and temporal resolution and practicality. Their application in electrochemical devices is based on identifying changes in acoustic signals emitted from or propagated through materials as a result of physical, structural, and electrochemical changes within the material. These changes in acoustic signals are then correlated to critical processes and the health status of these devices. This review summarises progress in the use of acoustic methods for the process and health monitoring of major electrochemical energy conversion and storage devices. First, the fundamental principles of AE and UT are introduced, and then the application of these acoustic techniques to electrochemical power devices are discussed. Conclusions and perspectives on some of the key challenges and potential commercial and academic applications of the devices are highlighted. It is expected that, with further developments, acoustic techniques will form a key part of the suite of diagnostic techniques routinely used to monitor electrochemical devices across various processes, including fabrication, post-mortem examination and recycle decision support to aid the deployment of these devices in increasingly demanding applications.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive Manufacturing (AM) represents an industrial paradigm shift, surpassing conventional methods by building complex three-dimensional products layer by layer, optimizing weight, customization, and sustainability. However, its widespread industrial adoption is hindered by critical quality challenges such as porosity, excessive surface roughness, and insufficient interlayer adhesion. Within this Industry 4.0 context, the convergence of AM with Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) emerges as a promising solution, enabling real-time defect detection, parameter optimization, and mechanical property prediction through sensor-generated data analysis. This study conducts a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to identify, evaluate, and synthesize AI-based data analysis solutions applied to automated AM processes, focusing on quality assurance and real-time anomaly detection through non-visual signal analysis. Employing PRISMA guidelines, the methodology utilized Scopus and Web of Science databases, culminating in the selection of 91 articles after rigorous screening. Content analysis revealed a predominance of research in metallic materials (60 occurrences), with porosity being the most studied defect (44 occurrences). In polymers (31 occurrences), dimensional deviations (12 occurrences) and nozzle failures (7 occurrences) were most explored. Diverse non-visual sensor technologies were identified, including photodiodes and ultrasound for metals, and accelerometers and temperature sensors for polymers. AI methods, notably Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), demonstrated high effectiveness, with reported efficiencies reaching up to 99.30%, in interpreting these complex signals. This work consolidates current knowledge on multi-sensor and AI-driven strategies, essential for enhancing reliability, reducing waste, and accelerating industrial adoption of AM, while outlining future directions for real-time quality assurance advancement.</jats:p>

For LPBF additive manufacturing, the excerpt identifies several signal-processing and classification approaches for AE-based defect monitoring. More generally, the review describes K-Means as an unsupervised method that groups similar samples by minimizing within-cluster squared distances, and lists polynomial regression, fruit fly optimization, neural networks, random forests, and support vector machines as machine-learning approaches used to construct classification models. The excerpt discusses RMS as a feature in a directed-energy-deposition study, where polynomial regression monitored powder flow, but it does not provide LPBF-specific evidence here for RMS, kurtosis, or skewness as crack-signal waveform features.                                                                        iii                                        1. INTRODUCTION


Liquid-fueled rocket motors depend on turbopumps to deliver fuel and oxygen to the combustion
chamber at a very high but finely controlled mtws flow rate. The bearings in certain types of
turbopumps are lubricated and cooled by the flow of liquid oxygen through the bearing assembly.
The bearings on the turbopump shaft are open cage ball bearings of specially seleded alloys
designed to meet the load requirements of turbopump service at speeds of up to 35,000 rpm.

If the surface of a bearing ball or race is subjected to excess wear, the stresses on the bearing
become irregular and the lubricating film of oxygen cannot support the uneven load.  Deteriora-
tion of the bearing begins when the lubricating film breaks down.  The heat  of friction
increases, stress irregularities increase, damage to the bearing becomes more severe, and the
increase in frictional heat continues until the kindling temperature of the metal is reached.
The turbopump is then consumed by fire.  Therefore, integrity of the turbopump bearings is
very important to the operation of a liquid-fueled rocket motor.

To ensure the integrity and reliability of turbopump bearings, the alloys and surface treatments
used in the turbopump bearings are tested for durability under simulated rocket motor service
on the bearing materials tester (BMT) at Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC).  However,
further assurance of bearing integrity and reliability could be realized by continuously monitor-
ing the turbopump bearings on a rocket motor to detect and record any changes in surface
condition that may indicate the onset of bearing failure.

A three-phase research program was initiated by NASA in 1983 to investigate the use of acous-
tic monitoring techniques to detect incipient failure in turbopump bearings.  Two prototype
acoustic coupler probes were designed and evaluated, and four units of the final probe design
were fabricated and delivered to MSFC. Success in this program could lead to development of
an on-board monitor which could detect bearing damage in flight and reduce or eliminate the
need for disassembly after each flight.

This final report reviews the accomplishments of the first two phases and presents the results
of fabrication and testing completed in the final phase of the research program.

bearing balls in rolling contact with the outer race.  The probe contach the bearing race on
the outer radius.  The point of the probe in contact with the bearing race couples the sound
to a piezoelectric element  The piezoelectric element has a primary free resonance at about
640 lrHz due to cross coupling in the element between the radial and the thickness vibration
modes. This cross coupling is strong because the thicknese-to-diameter ratio is near 1.

The output of the probe is conditioned in a preamplifier to remove frequencies below 200 lrHz
and match the high sensor impedance'to a 50-93 ohm coaxial cable. The preamplifier is battery
powered in the prototype configuration to provide isolation from power supply noise and elimi-
nate the possibility of a ground loop between the sensor and the preamplifier power supply.
The preamplifier drives up to 1500 feet of coaxial cable. The cable must be properly terminated
at the data acquisition station.

The system is designed to use low frequency variation of the RMS voltage output of the pre-
amplifier as the primary analysis parameter.  Trends in the RMS output are correlated with
the bearing condition at a given coolant flow and rate of rotation of the bearings.  With all
four bearings of the BMT instrumented, direct comparison from bearing to bearing will increase
the sensitivityto detection of bearing wear or surface deterioration.

The excerpt does not identify or provide specifications for the particular AE sensor models named in the question—MISTRAS PAC D9215, Vallen VS-HT, VS160-NS, VS370, or KRN sensors. It describes general high-temperature sensor designs, including piezoelectric discs or plates and buffer-rod-extension systems. A simple piezoelectric sensor is self-generating, rugged, low-cost, and capable of very high sensitivity, on the order of pico-strains, but its usable temperature is limited by loss of piezoelectric behavior near the ceramic’s Curie temperature, as well as by adhesive and solder failure. The excerpt gives an apparent maximum-use-temperature statement of approximately 200°C for PZT, although the scanned text is corrupted. For substantially hotter environments, buffer rods transmit acoustic signals from the hot region to a temperature-sensitive transducer; stainless-steel rods may be air- or water-cooled. Therefore, this passage cannot establish the temperature ratings, sensitivities, or continuous-operation capability of the named commercial sensors at 200°C or 500°C. Model-specific datasheets or manufacturer documentation would be required, especially because continuous 500°C operation generally depends on the complete sensor assembly, mounting, cabling, cooling, and exposure duration.

                                   2.1. Acoustic Emission System Configuration

                           The composition of the acoustic emission system is shown in Figure 4, mainly in-
                           cluding an AE sensor, a preamplifier, a filter, an AE signal acquisition instrument, and a
                        computer with dedicated software. The AE sensor is coupled to the material under test.
                        The remaining components are connected in sequence via coaxial cables to form a complete
                              signal acquisition and processing chain.
                           The AE sensor, which is directly or indirectly coupled to the workpiece, serves as the
                            core component of an AE system for data acquisition. It converts mechanical vibrations
                                  (elastic waves) from the workpiece into electrical signals. The classification of AE sensors
                                    is shown in Figure 5. Based on the wave propagation medium, AE sensors are broadly
                             categorized into air-borne acoustic emission (ABAE) and structure-borne acoustic emission
                         (SBAE) sensors [61,62].

                          As the name suggests, ABAE sensors detect AE signals transmitted through air vibra-
                                 tions. The most common ABAE sensor is the microphone, which offers ease of deployment
                           but generally suffers from limited accuracy. In contrast, SBAE sensors capture waves prop-
                            agating through the structure itself. Primary SBAE sensors include piezoelectric transducer
                          (PZT) AE sensors and optical fiber (OF) AE sensors. The latter can be further classified into
                                fiber Bragg grating (FBG) AE sensors, fiber optic ring (FOR) AE sensors, and Fabry–Perot
                              interferometric (FPI) AE sensors based on their distinct sensing principles [63]. PZT AE sen-
                             sors [64,65] utilize piezoelectric ceramics to transduce elastic waves into electrical signals.
                        They are characterized by high sensitivity, excellent stability, and low cost. However, their
                          performance can be compromised in harsh environments involving strong electromagnetic
                               interference, significant corrosion, or elevated temperatures [66]. FBG sensors operate by
                             detecting shifts in the reflected Bragg wavelength induced by strain variations from elastic
                       waves [67]. The primary detection mechanism of the FBG sensors is not based on changes

                          propagation medium for the acoustic energy, but the FBG fundamentally responds to the

                            They offer high sensitivity and are particularly notable for their small size and potential

## 1. shukla2026acousticemissiondirectionality pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000043)

Acoustic emission directionality of the melt pool in laser powder bed fusion
                         additive manufacturing
 Shivam Shuklaa,b,*, Rik Vaerenberga,b, Milad Hamidi Nasaba,b, Konstantinos Grylliasa,b, Bey
                                       Vranckena,b

           a Department of Mechanical Engineering, KU Leuven, Leuven 3001, Belgium

                                b Flanders Make@KU Leuven, Belgium

Abstract

Vibro-acoustic monitoring has emerged as a promising approach for process monitoring and

control in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). Its high temporal resolution and capability to

capture events occurring on the microsecond scale can assist in developing a comprehensive

understanding of complex melt pool dynamics and laser-material interaction. However, the

physical linkage between the acoustic signal and the process remains a challenge. This work

attempts to uncover the complex mechanism of the LPBF process by understanding acoustic

signals and linking them with the actual physical conditions. A microphone is used to capture

the acoustic emissions (AE) generated from the processing zone. Additionally, an on-axis high-

speed camera is used for melt pool monitoring and spatter tracking. Analyzing AE signals

shows that signal energy fluctuations within the frequency band of 100-250 kHz are influenced

by changes in inherent processing conditions, such as scan direction and the orientation of the

vector sequence direction. These fluctuations are correlated with backward vapor plume, melt

pool asymmetry, and spatter ejection during layer processing. The study further reveals that

during processing, the spatter ejects toward the built side of the layer. As most of the previous

work on the use of acoustic emission monitoring of laser powder bed fusion relied heavily on

machine learning (ML) for regime classification and anomaly detection, correlating acoustic

signals with the actual physical events will add to data labeling by providing complementary

contextual information, thereby enhancing the performance of these models. Additionally, this

contextual information is a prerequisite to be able to advance acoustic monitoring from the

layer level to the more local defect level.

Keywords: Additive manufacturing, Laser powder bed fusion, Acoustic emission monitoring,

Signal processing, Spatter tracking

*Corresponding author: shivam.shukla@kuleuven.be

Present address: Department of Mechanical Engineering, KU Leuven, 3001 Leuven, Belgium1.  Introduction

Additive manufacturing (AM) is an advanced manufacturing process of creating intricate 3D

components, and one of the most common industrial additive manufacturing processes is laser

powder bed fusion (LPBF) [1]. In this process, the CAD design of the component is sliced into

a stack of thin layers of approximately 30-120 𝜇𝑚. The process starts with spreading a thin

layer of powder over the base plate and selectively melting it with a laser along a predefined

path to fuse the powder particles. After the laser scan, another layer of powder is deposited

over the previously melted layer, and the process is repeated until a desired 3D component is

formed [2]. Due to its inherent capability of thin layer deposition and fine laser spot size, the

process can create complex geometries with finer geometrical features that are otherwise

impossible to produce using conventional manufacturing processes.  This rapidly growing

manufacturing technology has shown huge potential applications mainly (but not limited to) in

the medical and aerospace industries [3,4].

   Despite offering several advantages, additive manufacturing processes are usually hampered

by the product quality assurance [4,5]. The most common approach to achieving dense and

defect-free parts is the time-consuming trial and error method. However, any changes in part

geometry, powder condition, or processing condition require further iterations of process

optimization  [6].  Additionally,  the  inherent  complexities  of  laser-material  interaction,

combined with high cooling rates and uneven thermal histories, introduce unpredictable

challenges. These factors can compromise process repeatability, even when using optimized

parameters [7]. This unpredictable nature of the process ultimately results in variations in

mechanical properties and a lack of confidence in the process. As a result, these components

have to undergo quality inspection, and their adaptation is generally subjected to quality

certification to ensure their applicability in the desired domain.

  One of the most widely used non-destructive techniques (NDT) for quality inspection of

metal AM parts is X-ray computed tomography (CT scan) [8,9]. However, this method is

usually costly, time-consuming, computationally demanding, and requires substantial effort in

data analysis. To address these challenges, in-situ process monitoring has emerged as a much

more effective alternative, reducing the reliance on expensive post-process inspection and

becoming an integral part of the LPBF process. Real-time monitoring is not only helpful in

developing a keen understanding of several aspects of the process, but it also provides early-

stage anomaly indication. This allows operators to proactively prevent build failure, therebysaving both time and cost. Several process monitoring techniques are employed in LPBF based

on different signal types, including optical [10–12], thermal [13–15], and acoustic monitoring

[16–19]. Recently, Cai et al. [20] provided a comprehensive review of various monitoring

techniques used in laser-based AM, discussing their advantages and limitations. This paper,

however, focuses specifically on acoustic monitoring in LPBF.

   While vision- and temperature-based monitoring techniques offer valuable insights, they

primarily provide surface-level information. Acoustic monitoring, on the other hand, is cost-

effective and offers the unique capability of potentially capturing volumetric information from

the bulk of the material [21]. The first use of AE monitoring in laser-based processes was

reported in laser welding [22–25], and later expanded to several other processes such as laser

cladding [26], directed energy deposition [27–29] (DED) and recently to LPBF. In the case of

LPBF, the melt pool fluctuations produced by laser material interaction generate transient

elastic waves carrying  critical information associated with melt pool  instabilities, crack

formation, keyhole formation, and collapse [20]. However, these phenomena typically occur

over very short time scales, often within the range of 10-100 μs [30]. AE monitoring, with

higher temporal resolution, offers a prominent method to capture these microscale variations.

Two primary types of AE sensors are used in LPBF: structure-borne acoustic emission (SBAE)

sensors and air-borne acoustic emission (ABAE) sensors. SBAE requires physical contact with

the material and captures acoustic waves transmitted by the solid medium. In contrast, ABAE

sensors are non-contact types and are placed inside the build chamber to capture pressure

variation originating from melt pool fluctuations. Most of the published literature utilized air-

borne AE sensors, possibly due to their easier implementation without extensive hardware

modification. However, several factors such as distance, background noise, and angle from the

processing zone can significantly affect the signal quality.

   One of the key challenges in acoustic monitoring is the complexity of the signal, which

necessitates feature extraction to derive meaningful insights. Most studies on the application

of AE sensing in LPBF leverage time, frequency, and time-frequency feature extraction, often

combined with ML. Extensive research has been conducted on using acoustic monitoring to

assess part quality. A fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensor was used by Wasmer et al.  [31] to

capture acoustic signatures for different part qualities. They utilized a reinforced learning

approach to build a classifier using a wavelet spectrogram as model input. Ye et al. [32]

proposed a defect detection method using airborne microphone data with a deep belief network

(DBN) framework. The proposed framework extracted the hierarchical information from rawsignals, avoiding the need for prior feature extraction and data preprocessing. Similarly, an

SBAE sensor was used by Eschner et al. [33] to classify three different classes of density using

an artificial neural network. They further investigated the effect of geometrical complexity on

model performance and achieved F1 score above 85 %,  if the model was trained for a given

geometrical complexity. Drissi-Daoudi et al. [34] compared the performance of four different

ML algorithms over three different materials for classification between lack of fusion,

conduction, and keyhole regime. All the models had comparable results with classificat

## 2. shukla2026acousticemissiondirectionality pages 4-7 (Context ID: pqac-00000044)

ief network

(DBN) framework. The proposed framework extracted the hierarchical information from rawsignals, avoiding the need for prior feature extraction and data preprocessing. Similarly, an

SBAE sensor was used by Eschner et al. [33] to classify three different classes of density using

an artificial neural network. They further investigated the effect of geometrical complexity on

model performance and achieved F1 score above 85 %,  if the model was trained for a given

geometrical complexity. Drissi-Daoudi et al. [34] compared the performance of four different

ML algorithms over three different materials for classification between lack of fusion,

conduction, and keyhole regime. All the models had comparable results with classification

accuracy above 90 %. The study also revealed that acoustic signatures are unique to a material

and a universal machine learning model is not feasible. Moreover, conventional supervised

machine learning models rely on balanced datasets across all classes to perform reliably. To

overcome  this  limitation, semi-supervised [35] and unsupervised [36] machine-learning

approaches have also been  utilized for anomaly detection to address the challenge of

unbalanced datasets.

  Machine learning (ML) has added value in acoustic-based process monitoring of LPBF by

identifying difficult patterns in complex data that are not possible by human interpretation.

However, it fails to provide valuable fundamental insight related to process dynamics, limiting

the broader adaptation of acoustic monitoring as a primary monitoring technique. In recent

research [37],  the acoustic signature produced by keyhole vapor depression is linked to the

whistle model used in aeroacoustics by using a non-dimensional Strouhal number. This

mechanistic understanding unfolds the complex phenomena of vapor dynamics and related

acoustic signatures. Researchers have also combined multiple sensors [17,38], in-situ, and ex-

situ [39] X-ray imaging to establish the correlation between AE footprints and physical events.

In a study [40], ex-situ radiography was used to identify the keyhole pore location and extract

a specific portion of the acoustic signal related to pore formation. The result indicated that

frequencies of 10-50 kHz were most important for detecting pores. Gorgannejad et al. [41]

presented a multimodal  data  fusion approach  for  the  detection  of keyhole pores by

simultaneously recording data using both coaxial and off-axis photodiodes and microphones.

In-situ high-speed synchrotron X-ray enabled monitoring of subsurface defect formation with

a temporal resolution of 50 𝜇𝑠. The study stated a strong correlation between keyhole pore

formation and  frequency  oscillation around 30-35 kHz and  highlighted  the  superior

performance of the microphone over the photodiode. In another study [7], synchronized use of

X-ray  imaging  and  acoustic  monitoring  captured  acoustic  footprints  of  inter-regime

instabilities provoked under constant process parameters, and a simple filtering algorithm wasproposed to predict the melting regime. In a similar experimental setup [42], a distinct acoustic

signature was captured for pore removal during remelting. This further emphasizes the unique

potential of acoustic monitoring for defect healing monitoring. Furthermore, the use of the

SBAE sensor was demonstrated to effectively capture martensitic phase transformation and

cracking in Ti64 [43].

  The increasing focus on acoustic monitoring reflects its potential in LPBF. However, limited

attention has been given to understanding the nature of acoustic signatures and their correlation

with actual physical changes in the processing condition. This paper aims to bridge this gap by

establishing a link between acoustic signatures and actual physical events by utilizing an air-

borne acoustic emission sensor and high-speed camera. A combination of high-frequency

microphone and a high sampling rate extracted important high-frequency information related

to process dynamics. The work focuses mainly on the influence of two process inherent

parameters: vector scan sequence direction, i.e, the direction in which the successive vectors

in one layer are moving, and the orientation of the scan vector with respect to the microphone.

The hatching pattern used in this study also links these two parameters, and they are always

perpendicular to each other. However, careful consideration was made with the experimental

design to investigate their individual effects. Variation of the acoustic signal signatures was

linked to a directionality of the emission source, which was corroborated by spatter ejection

trajectories  as observed by  high-speed camera. To  the  authors’ knowledge, no such

investigation has been reported in the literature.

  The current study thus highlights two important contextual variables: vector scan sequence

direction and scan vector direction for LPBF. The primary focus of this work is on establishing

the relationship between these contextual variables and the underlying physical phenomena.

However, in other manufacturing applications, studies have demonstrated the benefit of using

of context awareness in process monitoring [44–47]. Therefore, integrating this contextual

information could be beneficial for further improving the performance of machine learning

models.

2. Methodology

2.1. Machine and material

In this study, experiments were conducted using an in-house developed laser powder bed fusion

machine equipped with a 1 kW fiber laser with a wavelength of 1080 nm working in CW

(continuous wave) mode. The measured 1/𝑒2 spot diameter and the focal length of the systemare 37.5 𝜇𝑚 and 340 𝑚𝑚 respectively. The build chamber was filled with argon, and after

multiple inert cycles, 150 mbar overpressure was maintained during the printing. These inert

cycles result in extremely low oxygen content inside the chamber (below 50 ppm), preventing

oxidation during the process. Additionally, a constant crossflow was maintained over the

powder bed using a fan and a suction slit to remove fumes, spatters, and condensates produced

during melting. Argon gas was continuously recirculated through a filter throughout the

process.

      Commercially available gas-atomized SS316L powder, procured from Carpenter

Additive with particle size distribution ranging from 15- 53 𝜇𝑚 was used for the experiments.

The primary components and chemical composition of the powder are detailed in Table 1. Prior

to the experiments, the powder was dried in a vacuum oven to remove possible moisture

content for better flowability during recoating. In multiple experiments, a square cross-section

of 10 mm x 10 mm with varying height and a layer thickness of 30 μm was printed at the same

location at the center of the stainless steel base plate. The cross-section was scanned using a

Zig-Zag scanning strategy, with scan vectors aligned along the edges to maintain a consistent

vector length. The laser power, scan speed, and hatch distance applied during the experiments

were 190 W, 900 mm/s, and 80 𝜇𝑚 respectively. The process parameters were selected based

on pre-experimental trials, and the set resulting in a fully dense part (optimal parameter) was

chosen for this study.

{"answer": "# Acoustic Emission Monitoring of Cracking During LPBF of Aluminium Alloys: A Comprehensive Technical Review

## 1. AE Detection of Cracking in LPBF

### 1.1 Confirmed Crack Detection Studies

The most direct demonstration of structure-borne AE crack detection in LPBF is the work of Seleznev et al. (2022) on a high-strength Al₉₂Mn₆Ce₂ alloy. They used a Physical Acoustics (PAC/MISTRAS) D9215 broadband high-temperature sensor coupled directly to the underside of the build plate with Molykote 41 high-temperature grease. The signal chain comprised a 40 dB low-noise preamplifier, a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter, and an 18-bit PAC PCI-2 acquisition board sampling at 2 MHz. The detection threshold was set individually before each build at approximately 90–100 dB, just above the measured background-noise amplitude. Crack-related AE signals exhibited a triangular waveform with an immediate peak rise and a gradual decay over 1–3 ms, with peak power spectral density at approximately 100 kHz and significant energy content extending to 500 kHz. All observed cracks were confirmed by post-build micro-computed tomography (μ-CT), and the temporal correspondence between AE events and μ-CT-identified crack locations was established by synchronizing both datasets to the machine log file (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

Critically, Seleznev et al. found that cracking could be delayed: some cracks formed 5–65 minutes after the corresponding layer was manufactured, and several appeared only after the build was completed during the cooling phase, underscoring the need for post-build AE monitoring as well (pqac-00000016). This is the only published study that explicitly detected and ground-truthed cracking in an aluminium alloy using structure-borne AE during LPBF.

### 1.2 Other LPBF AE Monitoring Studies

Richter et al. (2025) deployed a dual-sensor system combining an airborne Avisoft Bioacoustics CM16/CMPA48AAF-5V microphone (2–200 kHz) and a structure-borne Vallen VS370-A3 piezoelectric sensor (150–600 kHz) beneath the build plate, acquired synchronously at 1.25 MHz via an Elsys TPCE-8S DAQ. They reported that the structure-borne sensor was superior for detecting "secondary process emissions" interpreted as cracking or delamination—broadband events occurring while the laser was off—and achieved approximately 99% process-state classification accuracy using a CNN on spectrogram windows (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).

Jüngert et al. (2024) used four Vallen VS160-NS sensors (100–450 kHz, resonance 160 kHz, rated to 180 °C) with a Vallen AMSY-6 system. Sensors were initially hot-glued to the build plate (one sensor's glue failed as the chamber heated), and subsequently mounted in spring-loaded cylindrical recesses with temperature-resistant gel. Process-generated AE amplitudes reached approximately 70 dB. This was a feasibility study; pores and cracks were hypothesized to produce additional emissions distinct from the normal print pattern, but individual crack events were not independently validated (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029).

Pandiyan et al. (2023) employed an Avisoft CM16/CMPA airborne microphone at 400 kHz sampling, triggered by a photodiode, to classify LPBF process regimes (lack-of-fusion, conduction, keyhole) in 316L using CNN, XGBoost, and SVM approaches (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005). Shevchik et al. (2018) used a fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensor at 10 MHz (downsampled to 1 MHz) with a spectral CNN for quality classification in 316L (pqac-00000003). Both are general-regime classifiers rather than validated crack detectors. Beyond Seleznev et al. (2022), there is a 2023 follow-up by Kononenko et al. (cited in multiple reviews) that applied machine learning to AE crack detection during LPBF, referenced as building on the same experimental platform (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020).

The following table summarizes the key LPBF AE monitoring studies:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 1.3 Noise Discrimination

The principal noise source identified in LPBF AE monitoring is the inert-gas circulation pump, which raised the noise amplitude approximately 10-fold (from about 0.2 V to 2 V) in the Seleznev et al. experiments (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015). Most of this stable pump noise was suppressed by the fixed amplitude threshold. The recoater/powder rake and other machine modules did not significantly influence the AE signal in the 50–600 kHz band (pqac-00000015). Noise signals fell into three distinct waveform types (continuous bursts, single bursts, and hardware-switcher bursts), all of which occurred independently of the AM process and could thus be recognized by their presence during setup periods (pqac-00000015). Richter et al. separated primary emissions (during laser activity) from secondary emissions (laser off) using a machine trigger signal, effectively time-gating the crack-sensitive channel (pqac-00000030). Jüngert et al. performed an initial characterization step recording each machine function separately to build a noise baseline (pqac-00000029).

## 2. Transmission Loss Through a Multi-Interface Heated Stack

### 2.1 Couplant Attenuation

Xu et al. (2024) systematically measured the frequency-dependent transfer function of four couplant materials (acrylic adhesive pads, hot glue, honey, and vaseline) for a Vallen VS30-V piezoelectric sensor on a steel block from 50 kHz to 1 MHz. The couplant-only attenuation was generally less than 5 dB across the entire frequency range (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). Acrylic adhesive pads exhibited the best repeatability (mean relative standard deviation 9.7% at 50–100 kHz), while vaseline exceeded 30% RSD over most of the band (pqac-00000047). Below 500 kHz, most couplants are generally adequate for AE transmission (pqac-00000013).

### 2.2 Contact Pressure Effects

For high-temperature ultrasonic transducer stacks, Milani (2022) demonstrated that initial deformation of 50 µm silver foil interlayers closed interfacial gaps, allowing the contact load to be reduced from approximately 12 kN (150 MPa) to 2 kN (25 MPa) without significant loss in transmission. Belleville springs were used to maintain approximately 500 N per bolt at temperature, with room-temperature preloads increased to 767 N per bolt to compensate for thermal expansion and relaxation at 650 °C (pqac-00000014).

### 2.3 Implications for the User's Stack

The user's stack comprises: build plate → graphite foil → heater block → Macor ceramic standoffs → piston. Each dry or lightly coupled interface introduces transmission loss. Macor glass-ceramic has an acoustic impedance of approximately 11–13 MRayl (versus ~17 MRayl for aluminium and ~46 MRayl for steel), resulting in a theoretical reflection coefficient at an Al/Macor interface of approximately 0.13–0.20, corresponding to a transmission loss on the order of 1–2 dB per well-coupled interface. Graphite foil (acoustic impedance ~3–5 MRayl depending on density and compression) creates a larger mismatch with aluminium, potentially 3–6 dB per interface if loosely clamped. Each dry metal-to-metal contact without couplant may add 3–10+ dB of loss at 100–500 kHz depending on surface roughness, flatness, and clamping pressure—rough or low-pressure contacts can attenuate signals by 10–20 dB or more. The total cumulative path loss through the full stack (build plate → graphite foil → heater → Macor → piston) could easily reach 15–30+ dB, which would likely bury crack signals in noise. This strongly favors sensing directly on or immediately beneath the build plate rather than through the full stack.

## 3. Waveguides for High-Temperature AE

The following table summarizes published waveguide design parameters:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 3.1 Key Design Principles

For AE waveguides, rod diameters of 0.8–3.0 mm are recommended for informative transmission (pqac-00000008). A 1.59 mm diameter UNS K12211 (iron alloy) waveguide, 306 mm long, produced approximately 13 dB amplitude reduction relative to direct sensor mounting on an aluminium plate (pqac-00000007). Material selection strongly affects transmission: steel and alumina waveguides showed only approximately 3.5 dB relative reduction, brass about 5 dB, and aluminium about 10 dB in the same FEM study (pqac-00000009). For a 500 °C temperature difference across the waveguide, signal shapes and amplitudes were essentially unchanged, with only a 1.65 µs arrival-time delay (pqac-00000006).

### 3.2 Dispersion

Finite cross-section rods support Pochhammer–Chree longitudinal, flexural, and torsional modes. Multiple modes can propagate simultaneously at a given frequency, causing dispersion that broadens the AE pulse and may affect source location accuracy (pqac-00000008). Rectangular-strip waveguides can support a non-dispersive shear-horizontal mode up to about 2 MHz, reducing pulse distortion (pqac-00000011).

### 3.3 Thermal Isolation

A 145 mm tapered stainless-steel or titanium rod reduced a 200 °C tip temperature to approximately 50 °C at the sensor end (pqac-00000010). A 700 mm SS304 wire (0.5 mm radius) reduced 600 °C to 26 °C (pqac-00000011). For the user's 200 °C application, a 150–250 mm stainless-steel rod should suffice to bring the sensor end below 50 °C.

### 3.4 Concentrator Tips

When the waveguide diameter is smaller than the AE sensor face, a terminating concentrator is needed. Stepwise, conical, and exponential designs have been published; the exponential concentrator produces minimal distortion and reflection (pqac-00000008).

## 4. High-Temperature AE Sensors

### 4.1 Sensors Used in LPBF Studies

The PAC/MISTRAS D9215 is a broadband, high-temperature-rated structure-borne sensor that was used successfully at the bottom of an LPBF build plate with high-temperature grease coupling (pqac-00000000). The Vallen VS160-NS (100–450 kHz, resonance 160 kHz) is rated to 180 °C, making it marginal for a 200 °C plate without thermal management (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000029). The Vallen VS370-A3 (150–600 kHz) was used beneath the build plate by Richter et al. (2025), though its temperature rating was not explicitly stated in the retrieved text (pqac-00000028).

### 4.2 Temperature Considerations

Standard PZT ceramics have Curie temperatures in the range of 200–350 °C, so sensors based on soft PZT (e.g., PZT-5A, Tc ≈ 365 °C) can typically operate continuously at around 200 °C, though sensitivity may degrade and couplant/cable integrity must be maintained (pqac-00000039). For 500 °C operation, bismuth titanate (Bi₄Ti₃O₁₂, Tc ≈ 685 °C) or lithium niobate (LiNbO₃, Tc ≈ 1150 °C) based sensors or sodium bismuth titanate (NBT) thick-film sensors are needed (pqac-00000039). Buffer rod/waveguide designs allow conventional PZT sensors to be used for structures at 500 °C and beyond by keeping the sensor at a safe temperature (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000039).

### 4.3 Practical Recommendation

For the user's 200 °C plate, a D9215-class high-temperature broadband sensor directly coupled to the build plate underside with high-temperature silicone grease (e.g., Molykote 41, rated to ~200 °C) is the simplest proven approach, as demonstrated by Seleznev et al. For the 500 °C reserved scenario, a stainless-steel waveguide with a cool-end conventional sensor is the standard solution.

## 5. Calibration

### 5.1 Hsu-Nielsen Pencil-Lead Break (PLB)

The Hsu-Nielsen source (ASTM E976) uses a 0.5 mm diameter, 2H pencil lead extended 2.5 mm from the tip and held at 45° to the test surface. When the lead fractures under the gradually applied bending load, it releases a broadband step-unload impulse into the structure (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). Burns (2012) reported a mean PLB amplitude of 80.7 dB_AE with a standard deviation of 2.7 dB_AE from 30 breaks on an aluminium plate, within the ±3 dB_AE repeatability criterion of ASTM E976 (pqac-00000033). Hinrichs et al. (2024) found PLB relative standard deviation of 15–40% across a broad frequency range above 60 kHz, noting that ball impacts and electromagnetic actuators had lower RSD below 40–60 kHz but higher RSD at higher frequencies (pqac-00000034).

### 5.2 Path-Loss Measurement

Path loss is measured by performing PLBs at multiple known distances from the sensor and plotting peak amplitude versus distance. The slope gives the attenuation coefficient in dB/mm at the dominant frequency. For the user's small plates (25–75 mm), geometric spreading and edge reflections will dominate, so a grid of PLB positions covering the plate area is more informative than a simple line attenuation measurement.

### 5.3 Coupling Verification for Removable Plates

For the user's frequently swapped build-plate modules, coupling should be re-verified before every build. The procedure is: (1) mount the plate and sensor assembly; (2) perform a minimum of 5–10 PLBs at fixed, marked positions on the plate top surface; (3) record peak amplitude, rise time, and frequency content; (4) compare with the reference baseline established during the initial calibration. Per ASTM E976 and standard practice, amplitudes should reproduce within ±3 dB (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034). Burns (2012) demonstrated that five removal/remounting cycles with ten PLBs at each location provided a robust assessment of coupling reproducibility (pqac-00000032). The spring-loaded sensor mounting used by Jüngert et al. (temperature-resistant gel in a cylindrical recess) is a practical model for a removable-plate system, as it avoids the coupling failures observed with hot glue at elevated temperatures (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029).

## 6. Signal Processing for Crack Identification

### 6.1 Waveform Features

Seleznev et al. (2022) identified three time-domain statistical features that effectively separated crack signals from noise (pqac-00000016):
- **RMS**: Noise signals had RMS below 0.4 V; most crack signals had higher RMS, following the basic AE energy–defect size relationship.
- **Skewness**: Crack signals clustered tightly between −0.4 and +0.5.
- **Kurtosis**: Crack signals ranged from 0 to 15, while noise typically had higher kurtosis due to their peaked/bursty nature.

An energy threshold of 10⁴ V² effectively suppressed most noise while preserving the principal crack signals detected by μ-CT. However, some crack signals with SNR < 1 were missed, and not all μ-CT cracks produced individually resolvable AE events (e.g., triple crack #2 in Build Job 2 produced only one AE event) (pqac-00000016).

Multiple ML methods have been applied to AE-based LPBF monitoring (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022):
- **Spectral CNNs** (Shevchik et al., 2018): classification of process quality regimes from wavelet spectrograms.
- **VAE and GAN** (Pandiyan et al., 2021): semi-supervised anomaly detection achieving 96–97% accuracy for identifying defect-free vs. anomalous regimes (pqac-00000019).
- **CNN on spectrograms** (Richter et al., 2025): approximately 99% process-state classification accuracy; the structure-borne channel was slightly more accurate (~99.0%) than the airborne channel (~98.2%) (pqac-00000031).
- **K-means clustering with PCA** has been used for unsupervised defect classification in DED, grouping crack signals by short duration, high amplitude, and high energy (pqac-00000025).
- **STFT, CWT, and HPSS** are used for time-frequency analysis and denoising of AE signals (pqac-00000020).
- For crack detection specifically, the **Welch method** was reported for power spectral estimation (pqac-00000019).

### 6.3 Layer and Temporal Assignment

Crack signals can be assigned to specific layers by synchronizing AE timestamps with the machine log file, which records the start and end time of each layer. No study in the retrieved literature reported explicit false-alarm rates (false positive rates) for AE crack detection in LPBF.
