{"answer": "# Acoustic Emission Monitoring of Cracking During LPBF of Aluminium Alloys: A Comprehensive Technical Review

## 1. AE Detection of Cracking in LPBF

### 1.1 Confirmed Crack Detection Studies

The most direct demonstration of structure-borne AE crack detection in LPBF is the work of Seleznev et al. (2022) on a high-strength Al₉₂Mn₆Ce₂ alloy. They used a Physical Acoustics (PAC/MISTRAS) D9215 broadband high-temperature sensor coupled directly to the underside of the build plate with Molykote 41 high-temperature grease. The signal chain comprised a 40 dB low-noise preamplifier, a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter, and an 18-bit PAC PCI-2 acquisition board sampling at 2 MHz. The detection threshold was set individually before each build at approximately 90–100 dB, just above the measured background-noise amplitude. Crack-related AE signals exhibited a triangular waveform with an immediate peak rise and a gradual decay over 1–3 ms, with peak power spectral density at approximately 100 kHz and significant energy content extending to 500 kHz. All observed cracks were confirmed by post-build micro-computed tomography (μ-CT), and the temporal correspondence between AE events and μ-CT-identified crack locations was established by synchronizing both datasets to the machine log file (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

Critically, Seleznev et al. found that cracking could be delayed: some cracks formed 5–65 minutes after the corresponding layer was manufactured, and several appeared only after the build was completed during the cooling phase, underscoring the need for post-build AE monitoring as well (pqac-00000016). This is the only published study that explicitly detected and ground-truthed cracking in an aluminium alloy using structure-borne AE during LPBF.

### 1.2 Other LPBF AE Monitoring Studies

Richter et al. (2025) deployed a dual-sensor system combining an airborne Avisoft Bioacoustics CM16/CMPA48AAF-5V microphone (2–200 kHz) and a structure-borne Vallen VS370-A3 piezoelectric sensor (150–600 kHz) beneath the build plate, acquired synchronously at 1.25 MHz via an Elsys TPCE-8S DAQ. They reported that the structure-borne sensor was superior for detecting "secondary process emissions" interpreted as cracking or delamination—broadband events occurring while the laser was off—and achieved approximately 99% process-state classification accuracy using a CNN on spectrogram windows (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).

Jüngert et al. (2024) used four Vallen VS160-NS sensors (100–450 kHz, resonance 160 kHz, rated to 180 °C) with a Vallen AMSY-6 system. Sensors were initially hot-glued to the build plate (one sensor's glue failed as the chamber heated), and subsequently mounted in spring-loaded cylindrical recesses with temperature-resistant gel. Process-generated AE amplitudes reached approximately 70 dB. This was a feasibility study; pores and cracks were hypothesized to produce additional emissions distinct from the normal print pattern, but individual crack events were not independently validated (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029).

Pandiyan et al. (2023) employed an Avisoft CM16/CMPA airborne microphone at 400 kHz sampling, triggered by a photodiode, to classify LPBF process regimes (lack-of-fusion, conduction, keyhole) in 316L using CNN, XGBoost, and SVM approaches (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005). Shevchik et al. (2018) used a fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensor at 10 MHz (downsampled to 1 MHz) with a spectral CNN for quality classification in 316L (pqac-00000003). Both are general-regime classifiers rather than validated crack detectors. Beyond Seleznev et al. (2022), there is a 2023 follow-up by Kononenko et al. (cited in multiple reviews) that applied machine learning to AE crack detection during LPBF, referenced as building on the same experimental platform (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020).

The following table summarizes the key LPBF AE monitoring studies:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 1.3 Noise Discrimination

The principal noise source identified in LPBF AE monitoring is the inert-gas circulation pump, which raised the noise amplitude approximately 10-fold (from about 0.2 V to 2 V) in the Seleznev et al. experiments (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015). Most of this stable pump noise was suppressed by the fixed amplitude threshold. The recoater/powder rake and other machine modules did not significantly influence the AE signal in the 50–600 kHz band (pqac-00000015). Noise signals fell into three distinct waveform types (continuous bursts, single bursts, and hardware-switcher bursts), all of which occurred independently of the AM process and could thus be recognized by their presence during setup periods (pqac-00000015). Richter et al. separated primary emissions (during laser activity) from secondary emissions (laser off) using a machine trigger signal, effectively time-gating the crack-sensitive channel (pqac-00000030). Jüngert et al. performed an initial characterization step recording each machine function separately to build a noise baseline (pqac-00000029).

## 2. Transmission Loss Through a Multi-Interface Heated Stack

### 2.1 Couplant Attenuation

Xu et al. (2024) systematically measured the frequency-dependent transfer function of four couplant materials (acrylic adhesive pads, hot glue, honey, and vaseline) for a Vallen VS30-V piezoelectric sensor on a steel block from 50 kHz to 1 MHz. The couplant-only attenuation was generally less than 5 dB across the entire frequency range (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). Acrylic adhesive pads exhibited the best repeatability (mean relative standard deviation 9.7% at 50–100 kHz), while vaseline exceeded 30% RSD over most of the band (pqac-00000047). Below 500 kHz, most couplants are generally adequate for AE transmission (pqac-00000013).

### 2.2 Contact Pressure Effects

For high-temperature ultrasonic transducer stacks, Milani (2022) demonstrated that initial deformation of 50 µm silver foil interlayers closed interfacial gaps, allowing the contact load to be reduced from approximately 12 kN (150 MPa) to 2 kN (25 MPa) without significant loss in transmission. Belleville springs were used to maintain approximately 500 N per bolt at temperature, with room-temperature preloads increased to 767 N per bolt to compensate for thermal expansion and relaxation at 650 °C (pqac-00000014).

### 2.3 Implications for the User's Stack

The user's stack comprises: build plate → graphite foil → heater block → Macor ceramic standoffs → piston. Each dry or lightly coupled interface introduces transmission loss. Macor glass-ceramic has an acoustic impedance of approximately 11–13 MRayl (versus ~17 MRayl for aluminium and ~46 MRayl for steel), resulting in a theoretical reflection coefficient at an Al/Macor interface of approximately 0.13–0.20, corresponding to a transmission loss on the order of 1–2 dB per well-coupled interface. Graphite foil (acoustic impedance ~3–5 MRayl depending on density and compression) creates a larger mismatch with aluminium, potentially 3–6 dB per interface if loosely clamped. Each dry metal-to-metal contact without couplant may add 3–10+ dB of loss at 100–500 kHz depending on surface roughness, flatness, and clamping pressure—rough or low-pressure contacts can attenuate signals by 10–20 dB or more. The total cumulative path loss through the full stack (build plate → graphite foil → heater → Macor → piston) could easily reach 15–30+ dB, which would likely bury crack signals in noise. This strongly favors sensing directly on or immediately beneath the build plate rather than through the full stack.

## 3. Waveguides for High-Temperature AE

The following table summarizes published waveguide design parameters:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 3.1 Key Design Principles

For AE waveguides, rod diameters of 0.8–3.0 mm are recommended for informative transmission (pqac-00000008). A 1.59 mm diameter UNS K12211 (iron alloy) waveguide, 306 mm long, produced approximately 13 dB amplitude reduction relative to direct sensor mounting on an aluminium plate (pqac-00000007). Material selection strongly affects transmission: steel and alumina waveguides showed only approximately 3.5 dB relative reduction, brass about 5 dB, and aluminium about 10 dB in the same FEM study (pqac-00000009). For a 500 °C temperature difference across the waveguide, signal shapes and amplitudes were essentially unchanged, with only a 1.65 µs arrival-time delay (pqac-00000006).

### 3.2 Dispersion

Finite cross-section rods support Pochhammer–Chree longitudinal, flexural, and torsional modes. Multiple modes can propagate simultaneously at a given frequency, causing dispersion that broadens the AE pulse and may affect source location accuracy (pqac-00000008). Rectangular-strip waveguides can support a non-dispersive shear-horizontal mode up to about 2 MHz, reducing pulse distortion (pqac-00000011).

### 3.3 Thermal Isolation

A 145 mm tapered stainless-steel or titanium rod reduced a 200 °C tip temperature to approximately 50 °C at the sensor end (pqac-00000010). A 700 mm SS304 wire (0.5 mm radius) reduced 600 °C to 26 °C (pqac-00000011). For the user's 200 °C application, a 150–250 mm stainless-steel rod should suffice to bring the sensor end below 50 °C.

### 3.4 Concentrator Tips

When the waveguide diameter is smaller than the AE sensor face, a terminating concentrator is needed. Stepwise, conical, and exponential designs have been published; the exponential concentrator produces minimal distortion and reflection (pqac-00000008).

## 4. High-Temperature AE Sensors

### 4.1 Sensors Used in LPBF Studies

The PAC/MISTRAS D9215 is a broadband, high-temperature-rated structure-borne sensor that was used successfully at the bottom of an LPBF build plate with high-temperature grease coupling (pqac-00000000). The Vallen VS160-NS (100–450 kHz, resonance 160 kHz) is rated to 180 °C, making it marginal for a 200 °C plate without thermal management (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000029). The Vallen VS370-A3 (150–600 kHz) was used beneath the build plate by Richter et al. (2025), though its temperature rating was not explicitly stated in the retrieved text (pqac-00000028).

### 4.2 Temperature Considerations

Standard PZT ceramics have Curie temperatures in the range of 200–350 °C, so sensors based on soft PZT (e.g., PZT-5A, Tc ≈ 365 °C) can typically operate continuously at around 200 °C, though sensitivity may degrade and couplant/cable integrity must be maintained (pqac-00000039). For 500 °C operation, bismuth titanate (Bi₄Ti₃O₁₂, Tc ≈ 685 °C) or lithium niobate (LiNbO₃, Tc ≈ 1150 °C) based sensors or sodium bismuth titanate (NBT) thick-film sensors are needed (pqac-00000039). Buffer rod/waveguide designs allow conventional PZT sensors to be used for structures at 500 °C and beyond by keeping the sensor at a safe temperature (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000039).

### 4.3 Practical Recommendation

For the user's 200 °C plate, a D9215-class high-temperature broadband sensor directly coupled to the build plate underside with high-temperature silicone grease (e.g., Molykote 41, rated to ~200 °C) is the simplest proven approach, as demonstrated by Seleznev et al. For the 500 °C reserved scenario, a stainless-steel waveguide with a cool-end conventional sensor is the standard solution.

## 5. Calibration

### 5.1 Hsu-Nielsen Pencil-Lead Break (PLB)

The Hsu-Nielsen source (ASTM E976) uses a 0.5 mm diameter, 2H pencil lead extended 2.5 mm from the tip and held at 45° to the test surface. When the lead fractures under the gradually applied bending load, it releases a broadband step-unload impulse into the structure (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). Hinrichs et al. (2024) found PLB relative standard deviation of 15–40% across a broad frequency range above 60 kHz, noting that ball impacts and electromagnetic actuators had lower RSD below 40–60 kHz but higher RSD at higher frequencies (pqac-00000034).

### 5.2 Path-Loss Measurement

Path loss is measured by performing PLBs at multiple known distances from the sensor and plotting peak amplitude versus distance. The slope gives the attenuation coefficient in dB/mm at the dominant frequency. For the user's small plates (25–75 mm), geometric spreading and edge reflections will dominate, so a grid of PLB positions covering the plate area is more informative than a simple line attenuation measurement.

For the user's frequently swapped build-plate modules, coupling should be re-verified before every build. Context: we are designing a lab-built desktop laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for small-batch screening of aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, 6061, 7075 and grain-refined variants with Zr, Sc or TiB2). Laser: 500 W single-mode CW fibre laser at 1070 nm (IPG YLR-500 class) into a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (marking speed up to about 1.1 m/s at f = 160 mm) and a Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta lens (f = 160 mm), giving a ~96 um 1/e2 spot diameter (48-75 um spots are options). Expected process window: 200-350 W, 0.4-1.1 m/s, 30 um layers, ~0.1 mm hatch. Build plates are 25, 50 or 75 mm across, heated to 200 C (500 C reserved). Chamber: ~280 x 190 x 120 mm inside, vacuum-purged then argon at +5 to +20 mbar, with an argon cross-flow of 2.5-3.3 m/s over the plate (140-200 L/min) from a slot nozzle on the back wall to an outlet slot at the front; a cover slide sits under a lid window ~130 mm above the plate.

We want acoustic emission (AE) monitoring of cracking during LPBF of crack-prone aluminium alloys (6061, 7075). The build plate (25-75 mm across, 6061) sits on graphite foil on a heater block (200 C, up to 500 C later) that stands on three Macor ceramic standoffs on a piston with a hollow rod; the piston slides in a bore sealed by an O-ring, and the module is swapped often.

1. AE in LPBF: which papers detected cracking (hot or cold) with structure-borne AE; sensor types and models, frequency bands, sampling rates, preamp gains and thresholds; how they told crack signals from recoater, gas-flow and pump noise. Any for Al alloys besides Seleznev et al. 2022?
2. Mounting through a heated, multi-interface stack: transmission loss across dry or bolted contacts, graphite foil and ceramic standoffs; typical dB loss per interface at 100-500 kHz; how contact pressure and couplants (high-temperature grease, gold or aluminium foil) change it.
3. Waveguides for high-temperature AE: rod diameter, material, length, tip and contact design, spring force, dispersion (Pochhammer-Chree modes) and attenuation at 100-500 kHz; published designs (welding, nuclear, LPBF heated plates) and how much signal they lose against direct mounting.
4. High-temperature AE sensors (MISTRAS/PAC D9215, Vallen VS-HT series, KRN and others): temperature ratings and sensitivities; whether a sensor can sit on a 200 C plate.
5. Calibration: Hsu-Nielsen pencil-lead breaks, path-loss measurement, and how often a removable plate's acoustic coupling should be re-checked.
6. Signal processing used to place cracks in time and layer: waveform features, clustering, machine learning; false-alarm rates where reported.

Give quantitative values and sources.

Context: we are designing a lab-built desktop laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for small-batch screening of aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, 6061, 7075 and grain-refined variants with Zr, Sc or TiB2). Laser: 500 W single-mode CW fibre laser at 1070 nm (IPG YLR-500 class) into a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (marking speed up to about 1.1 m/s at f = 160 mm) and a Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta lens (f = 160 mm), giving a ~96 um 1/e2 spot diameter (48-75 um spots are options). Expected process window: 200-350 W, 0.4-1.1 m/s, 30 um layers, ~0.1 mm hatch. Build plates are 25, 50 or 75 mm across, heated to 200 C (500 C reserved). Chamber: ~280 x 190 x 120 mm inside, vacuum-purged then argon at +5 to +20 mbar, with an argon cross-flow of 2.5-3.3 m/s over the plate (140-200 L/min) from a slot nozzle on the back wall to an outlet slot at the front; a cover slide sits under a lid window ~130 mm above the plate.

We want acoustic emission (AE) monitoring of cracking during LPBF of crack-prone aluminium alloys (6061, 7075). The build plate (25-75 mm across, 6061) sits on graphite foil on a heater block (200 C, up to 500 C later) that stands on three Macor ceramic standoffs on a piston with a hollow rod; the piston slides in a bore sealed by an O-ring, and the module is swapped often.

1. AE in LPBF: which papers detected cracking (hot or cold) with structure-borne AE; sensor types and models, frequency bands, sampling rates, preamp gains and thresholds; how they told crack signals from recoater, gas-flow and pump noise. Any for Al alloys besides Seleznev et al. 2022?
2. Mounting through a heated, multi-interface stack: transmission loss across dry or bolted contacts, graphite foil and ceramic standoffs; typical dB loss per interface at 100-500 kHz; how contact pressure and couplants (high-temperature grease, gold or aluminium foil) change it.
3. Waveguides for high-temperature AE: rod diameter, material, length, tip and contact design, spring force, dispersion (Pochhammer-Chree modes) and attenuation at 100-500 kHz; published designs (welding, nuclear, LPBF heated plates) and how much signal they lose against direct mounting.
4. High-temperature AE sensors (MISTRAS/PAC D9215, Vallen VS-HT series, KRN and others): temperature ratings and sensitivities; whether a sensor can sit on a 200 C plate.
5. Calibration: Hsu-Nielsen pencil-lead breaks, path-loss measurement, and how often a removable plate's acoustic coupling should be re-checked.
6. Signal processing used to place cracks in time and layer: waveform features, clustering, machine learning; false-alarm rates where reported.

Give quantitative values and sources.
answer.answer:
# Acoustic Emission Monitoring of Cracking During LPBF of Aluminium Alloys: A Comprehensive Technical Review

## 1. AE Detection of Cracking in LPBF

### 1.1 Confirmed Crack Detection Studies

The most direct demonstration of structure-borne AE crack detection in LPBF is the work of Seleznev et al. (2022) on a high-strength Al₉₂Mn₆Ce₂ alloy. They used a Physical Acoustics (PAC/MISTRAS) D9215 broadband high-temperature sensor coupled directly to the underside of the build plate with Molykote 41 high-temperature grease. The signal chain comprised a 40 dB low-noise preamplifier, a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter, and an 18-bit PAC PCI-2 acquisition board sampling at 2 MHz. The detection threshold was set individually before each build at approximately 90–100 dB, just above the measured background-noise amplitude. Crack-related AE signals exhibited a triangular waveform with an immediate peak rise and a gradual decay over 1–3 ms, with peak power spectral density at approximately 100 kHz and significant energy content extending to 500 kHz. All observed cracks were confirmed by post-build micro-computed tomography (μ-CT), and the temporal correspondence between AE events and μ-CT-identified crack locations was established by synchronizing both datasets to the machine log file (seleznev2022insitudetection pages 2-3, seleznev2022insitudetection pages 3-5, seleznev2022insitudetection pages 5-7).

Critically, Seleznev et al. found that cracking could be delayed: some cracks formed 5–65 minutes after the corresponding layer was manufactured, and several appeared only after the build was completed during the cooling phase, underscoring the need for post-build AE monitoring as well (seleznev2022insitudetection pages 5-7). This is the only published study that explicitly detected and ground-truthed cracking in an aluminium alloy using structure-borne AE during LPBF.

### 1.2 Other LPBF AE Monitoring Studies

Richter et al. (2025) deployed a dual-sensor system combining an airborne Avisoft Bioacoustics CM16/CMPA48AAF-5V microphone (2–200 kHz) and a structure-borne Vallen VS370-A3 piezoelectric sensor (150–600 kHz) beneath the build plate, acquired synchronously at 1.25 MHz via an Elsys TPCE-8S DAQ. They reported that the structure-borne sensor was superior for detecting "secondary process emissions" interpreted as cracking or delamination—broadband events occurring while the laser was off—and achieved approximately 99% process-state classification accuracy using a CNN on spectrogram windows (richter2025finedetectionof pages 1-3, richter2025finedetectionof pages 3-5, richter2025finedetectionof pages 5-7).

Jüngert et al. (2024) used four Vallen VS160-NS sensors (100–450 kHz, resonance 160 kHz, rated to 180 °C) with a Vallen AMSY-6 system. Sensors were initially hot-glued to the build plate (one sensor's glue failed as the chamber heated), and subsequently mounted in spring-loaded cylindrical recesses with temperature-resistant gel. Process-generated AE amplitudes reached approximately 70 dB. This was a feasibility study; pores and cracks were hypothesized to produce additional emissions distinct from the normal print pattern, but individual crack events were not independently validated (jungert2024acousticemissionmonitoring pages 1-3, jungert2024acousticemissionmonitoring pages 3-8).

Pandiyan et al. (2023) employed an Avisoft CM16/CMPA airborne microphone at 400 kHz sampling, triggered by a photodiode, to classify LPBF process regimes (lack-of-fusion, conduction, keyhole) in 316L using CNN, XGBoost, and SVM approaches (pandiyan2023optimizinginsitumonitoring pages 3-4, pandiyan2023optimizinginsitumonitoring pages 4-5). Shevchik et al. (2018) used a fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensor at 10 MHz (downsampled to 1 MHz) with a spectral CNN for quality classification in 316L (shevchik2018acousticemissionfor pages 5-7). Both are general-regime classifiers rather than validated crack detectors. Beyond Seleznev et al. (2022), there is a 2023 follow-up by Kononenko et al. (cited in multiple reviews) that applied machine learning to AE crack detection during LPBF, referenced as building on the same experimental platform (chang2026areviewof pages 22-23, nobari2026mechanismssensorsand pages 9-11).

### 1.3 Noise Discrimination

The principal noise source identified in LPBF AE monitoring is the inert-gas circulation pump, which raised the noise amplitude approximately 10-fold (from about 0.2 V to 2 V) in the Seleznev et al. experiments (seleznev2022insitudetection pages 2-3, seleznev2022insitudetection pages 3-5). Most of this stable pump noise was suppressed by the fixed amplitude threshold. The recoater/powder rake and other machine modules did not significantly influence the AE signal in the 50–600 kHz band (seleznev2022insitudetection pages 3-5). Noise signals fell into three distinct waveform types (continuous bursts, single bursts, and hardware-switcher bursts), all of which occurred independently of the AM process and could thus be recognized by their presence during setup periods (seleznev2022insitudetection pages 3-5). Richter et al. separated primary emissions (during laser activity) from secondary emissions (laser off) using a machine trigger signal, effectively time-gating the crack-sensitive channel (richter2025finedetectionof pages 3-5). Jüngert et al. performed an initial characterization step recording each machine function separately to build a noise baseline (jungert2024acousticemissionmonitoring pages 1-3).

## 2. Transmission Loss Through a Multi-Interface Heated Stack

### 2.1 Couplant Attenuation

Xu et al. (2024) systematically measured the frequency-dependent transfer function of four couplant materials (acrylic adhesive pads, hot glue, honey, and vaseline) for a Vallen VS30-V piezoelectric sensor on a steel block from 50 kHz to 1 MHz. The couplant-only attenuation was generally less than 5 dB across the entire frequency range (xu2024frequencydependentamplitude pages 5-6, xu2024frequencydependentamplitude pages 6-9). Acrylic adhesive pads exhibited the best repeatability (mean relative standard deviation 9.7% at 50–100 kHz), while vaseline exceeded 30% RSD over most of the band (xu2024frequencydependentamplitude pages 5-6). Below 500 kHz, most couplants are generally adequate for AE transmission (brunner2021structuralhealthand pages 5-6).

### 2.2 Contact Pressure Effects

For high-temperature ultrasonic transducer stacks, Milani (2022) demonstrated that initial deformation of 50 µm silver foil interlayers closed interfacial gaps, allowing the contact load to be reduced from approximately 12 kN (150 MPa) to 2 kN (25 MPa) without significant loss in transmission. Belleville springs were used to maintain approximately 500 N per bolt at temperature, with room-temperature preloads increased to 767 N per bolt to compensate for thermal expansion and relaxation at 650 °C (milani2022designandmanufacturinga pages 28-33).

### 2.3 Implications for the User's Stack

The user's stack comprises: build plate → graphite foil → heater block → Macor ceramic standoffs → piston. Each dry or lightly coupled interface introduces transmission loss. Macor glass-ceramic has an acoustic impedance of approximately 11–13 MRayl (versus ~17 MRayl for aluminium and ~46 MRayl for steel), resulting in a theoretical reflection coefficient at an Al/Macor interface of approximately 0.13–0.20, corresponding to a transmission loss on the order of 1–2 dB per well-coupled interface. Graphite foil (acoustic impedance ~3–5 MRayl depending on density and compression) creates a larger mismatch with aluminium, potentially 3–6 dB per interface if loosely clamped. Each dry metal-to-metal contact without couplant may add 3–10+ dB of loss at 100–500 kHz depending on surface roughness, flatness, and clamping pressure—rough or low-pressure contacts can attenuate signals by 10–20 dB or more. The total cumulative path loss through the full stack (build plate → graphite foil → heater → Macor → piston) could easily reach 15–30+ dB, which would likely bury crack signals in noise. This strongly favors sensing directly on or immediately beneath the build plate rather than through the full stack.

### 3.1 Key Design Principles

For AE waveguides, rod diameters of 0.8–3.0 mm are recommended for informative transmission (zakharov2010acousticemissionsignal pages 1-5). A 1.59 mm diameter UNS K12211 (iron alloy) waveguide, 306 mm long, produced approximately 13 dB amplitude reduction relative to direct sensor mounting on an aluminium plate (zelenyak2015modelingofacoustic pages 1-4). Material selection strongly affects transmission: steel and alumina waveguides showed only approximately 3.5 dB relative reduction, brass about 5 dB, and aluminium about 10 dB in the same FEM study (zelenyak2015modelingofacoustic pages 11-15). For a 500 °C temperature difference across the waveguide, signal shapes and amplitudes were essentially unchanged, with only a 1.65 µs arrival-time delay (zelenyak2015modelingofacoustic pages 15-18).

### 3.2 Dispersion

Finite cross-section rods support Pochhammer–Chree longitudinal, flexural, and torsional modes. Multiple modes can propagate simultaneously at a given frequency, causing dispersion that broadens the AE pulse and may affect source location accuracy (zakharov2010acousticemissionsignal pages 1-5). Rectangular-strip waveguides can support a non-dispersive shear-horizontal mode up to about 2 MHz, reducing pulse distortion (kazys2021hightemperatureultrasonic pages 9-11).

### 3.3 Thermal Isolation

A 145 mm tapered stainless-steel or titanium rod reduced a 200 °C tip temperature to approximately 50 °C at the sensor end (kazys2021hightemperatureultrasonic pages 7-9). A 700 mm SS304 wire (0.5 mm radius) reduced 600 °C to 26 °C (kazys2021hightemperatureultrasonic pages 9-11). For the user's 200 °C application, a 150–250 mm stainless-steel rod should suffice to bring the sensor end below 50 °C.

### 3.4 Concentrator Tips

When the waveguide diameter is smaller than the AE sensor face, a terminating concentrator is needed. Stepwise, conical, and exponential designs have been published; the exponential concentrator produces minimal distortion and reflection (zakharov2010acousticemissionsignal pages 1-5).

## 4. High-Temperature AE Sensors

### 4.1 Sensors Used in LPBF Studies

The PAC/MISTRAS D9215 is a broadband, high-temperature-rated structure-borne sensor that was used successfully at the bottom of an LPBF build plate with high-temperature grease coupling (seleznev2022insitudetection pages 2-3). The Vallen VS160-NS (100–450 kHz, resonance 160 kHz) is rated to 180 °C, making it marginal for a 200 °C plate without thermal management (jungert2024acousticemissionmonitoring pages 1-3). The Vallen VS370-A3 (150–600 kHz) was used beneath the build plate by Richter et al. (2025), though its temperature rating was not explicitly stated in the retrieved text (richter2025finedetectionof pages 1-3).

### 4.2 Temperature Considerations

Standard PZT ceramics have Curie temperatures in the range of 200–350 °C, so sensors based on soft PZT (e.g., PZT-5A, Tc ≈ 365 °C) can typically operate continuously at around 200 °C, though sensitivity may degrade and couplant/cable integrity must be maintained (shrout1993hightemperaturesensormicrophone pages 148-151). For 500 °C operation, bismuth titanate (Bi₄Ti₃O₁₂, Tc ≈ 685 °C) or lithium niobate (LiNbO₃, Tc ≈ 1150 °C) based sensors or sodium bismuth titanate (NBT) thick-film sensors are needed (shrout1993hightemperaturesensormicrophone pages 148-151). Buffer rod/waveguide designs allow conventional PZT sensors to be used for structures at 500 °C and beyond by keeping the sensor at a safe temperature (shrout1993hightemperaturesensormicrophone pages 148-151).

### 4.3 Practical Recommendation

For the user's 200 °C plate, a D9215-class high-temperature broadband sensor directly coupled to the build plate underside with high-temperature silicone grease (e.g., Molykote 41, rated to ~200 °C) is the simplest proven approach, as demonstrated by Seleznev et al. For the 500 °C reserved scenario, a stainless-steel waveguide with a cool-end conventional sensor is the standard solution.

## 5. Calibration

### 5.1 Hsu-Nielsen Pencil-Lead Break (PLB)

The Hsu-Nielsen source (ASTM E976) uses a 0.5 mm diameter, 2H pencil lead extended 2.5 mm from the tip and held at 45° to the test surface. When the lead fractures under the gradually applied bending load, it releases a broadband step-unload impulse into the structure (jolly1994investigationofacoustic pages 1-6, jolly1994investigationofacoustic pages 10-12). Burns (2012) reported a mean PLB amplitude of 80.7 dB_AE with a standard deviation of 2.7 dB_AE from 30 breaks on an aluminium plate, within the ±3 dB_AE repeatability criterion of ASTM E976 (burns2012developmentandcharacterisation pages 170-174). Hinrichs et al. (2024) found PLB relative standard deviation of 15–40% across a broad frequency range above 60 kHz, noting that ball impacts and electromagnetic actuators had lower RSD below 40–60 kHz but higher RSD at higher frequencies (hinrichs2024analysisofthe pages 1-3).

### 5.2 Path-Loss Measurement

Path loss is measured by performing PLBs at multiple known distances from the sensor and plotting peak amplitude versus distance. The slope gives the attenuation coefficient in dB/mm at the dominant frequency. For the user's small plates (25–75 mm), geometric spreading and edge reflections will dominate, so a grid of PLB positions covering the plate area is more informative than a simple line attenuation measurement.

### 5.3 Coupling Verification for Removable Plates

For the user's frequently swapped build-plate modules, coupling should be re-verified before every build. The procedure is: (1) mount the plate and sensor assembly; (2) perform a minimum of 5–10 PLBs at fixed, marked positions on the plate top surface; (3) record peak amplitude, rise time, and frequency content; (4) compare with the reference baseline established during the initial calibration. Per ASTM E976 and standard practice, amplitudes should reproduce within ±3 dB (burns2012developmentandcharacterisation pages 170-174, hinrichs2024analysisofthe pages 1-3). Burns (2012) demonstrated that five removal/remounting cycles with ten PLBs at each location provided a robust assessment of coupling reproducibility (burns2012developmentandcharacterisation pages 115-120). The spring-loaded sensor mounting used by Jüngert et al. (temperature-resistant gel in a cylindrical recess) is a practical model for a removable-plate system, as it avoids the coupling failures observed with hot glue at elevated temperatures (jungert2024acousticemissionmonitoring pages 3-8, jungert2024acousticemissionmonitoring pages 1-3).

## 6. Signal Processing for Crack Identification

### 6.1 Waveform Features

Seleznev et al. (2022) identified three time-domain statistical features that effectively separated crack signals from noise (seleznev2022insitudetection pages 5-7):
- **RMS**: Noise signals had RMS below 0.4 V; most crack signals had higher RMS, following the basic AE energy–defect size relationship.
- **Skewness**: Crack signals clustered tightly between −0.4 and +0.5.
- **Kurtosis**: Crack signals ranged from 0 to 15, while noise typically had higher kurtosis due to their peaked/bursty nature.

An energy threshold of 10⁴ V² effectively suppressed most noise while preserving the principal crack signals detected by μ-CT. However, some crack signals with SNR < 1 were missed, and not all μ-CT cracks produced individually resolvable AE events (e.g., triple crack #2 in Build Job 2 produced only one AE event) (seleznev2022insitudetection pages 5-7).

### 6.2 Machine Learning Approaches

Multiple ML methods have been applied to AE-based LPBF monitoring (chang2026areviewof pages 22-23, nobari2026mechanismssensorsand pages 9-11, chang2026areviewof pages 16-19):
- **Spectral CNNs** (Shevchik et al., 2018): classification of process quality regimes from wavelet spectrograms.
- **VAE and GAN** (Pandiyan et al., 2021): semi-supervised anomaly detection achieving 96–97% accuracy for identifying defect-free vs. anomalous regimes (chang2026areviewof pages 22-23).
- **CNN on spectrograms** (Richter et al., 2025): approximately 99% process-state classification accuracy; the structure-borne channel was slightly more accurate (~99.0%) than the airborne channel (~98.2%) (richter2025finedetectionof pages 5-7).
- **K-means clustering with PCA** has been used for unsupervised defect classification in DED, grouping crack signals by short duration, high amplitude, and high energy (nobari2026mechanismssensorsand pages 11-12).
- **STFT, CWT, and HPSS** are used for time-frequency analysis and denoising of AE signals (nobari2026mechanismssensorsand pages 9-11).
- For crack detection specifically, the **Welch method** was reported for power spectral estimation (chang2026areviewof pages 22-23).

### 6.3 Layer and Temporal Assignment

Crack signals can be assigned to specific layers by synchronizing AE timestamps with the machine log file, which records the start and end time of each layer. Seleznev et al. demonstrated this by plotting AE events on the build timeline and correlating them with μ-CT crack heights, finding delays of minutes to over an hour between layer deposition and crack formation (seleznev2022insitudetection pages 3-5, seleznev2022insitudetection pages 5-7). Richter et al. used a machine trigger to separate laser-on and laser-off intervals, assigning secondary emissions to inter-layer cooling periods (richter2025finedetectionof pages 3-5).

### 6.4 False-Alarm Rates

No study in the retrieved literature reported explicit false-alarm rates (false positive rates) for AE crack detection in LPBF. Seleznev et al. noted that some pump-noise bursts exceeded the threshold and would constitute false alarms without additional waveform classification; they recommended either physically isolating the pump or implementing threshold-free monitoring with ML classification as a future goal (seleznev2022insitudetection pages 5-7). The semi-supervised approaches of Pandiyan et al. (2021) reported 96–97% accuracy for anomaly detection but did not decompose this into precision and recall for cracks specifically (chang2026areviewof pages 22-23). This remains an open area requiring further work, particularly for crack-prone aluminium alloys where the number of genuine crack events may be small relative to noise events.

## Summary and Recommendations for the User's System

For the described lab-built LPBF machine targeting crack-prone 6061 and 7075 aluminium alloys:

1. **Sensor selection**: A MISTRAS/PAC D9215 or equivalent broadband high-temperature sensor (50–600 kHz) mounted directly beneath the build plate is the proven configuration for crack AE at 200 °C. The Vallen VS160-NS (rated 180 °C) is a viable alternative if thermally managed.

2. **Mounting**: Couple the sensor to the build plate underside using high-temperature silicone grease (Molykote 41 or equivalent). A spring-loaded recess in the plate is recommended for removability and thermal robustness, following the Jüngert et al. design. Avoid routing the AE signal through the full graphite-foil/heater/Macor/piston stack, as cumulative interface losses could exceed 15–30 dB.

3. **Acquisition**: Sample at ≥2 MHz, 18-bit, with 40 dB preamplifier gain and a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter. Set the threshold just above the background with the gas system running (expect the argon circulation pump to be the dominant noise source).

4. **Waveguide option**: For the 500 °C reserved scenario, a 1.5–2 mm diameter, 150–250 mm long 304/316 stainless-steel rod with a polished flat tip, 10–20 N spring preload, and an exponential concentrator at the cool end is a practical starting design, with an expected insertion loss of 5–15 dB.

5. **Calibration**: Perform Hsu-Nielsen PLBs (0.5 mm 2H lead, 2.5 mm extension, 45°) at 5–10 fixed positions before every build. Compare peak amplitudes to a reference baseline within ±3 dB to verify coupling.

6. **Signal processing**: Use waveform shape (triangular, 1–3 ms decay), RMS, skewness (−0.4 to 0.5), and kurtosis (0–15) for initial crack/noise separation. Synchronize AE timestamps to the layer log. Continue monitoring for at least one hour after build completion to capture delayed cracking. For automated classification, CNN-based approaches on spectrograms have achieved approximately 99% accuracy for process-state discrimination.

# Acoustic Emission Monitoring of Cracking During LPBF of Aluminium Alloys: A Comprehensive Technical Review

## 1. AE Detection of Cracking in LPBF

### 1.1 Confirmed Crack Detection Studies

The most direct demonstration of structure-borne AE crack detection in LPBF is the work of Seleznev et al. (2022) on a high-strength Al₉₂Mn₆Ce₂ alloy. They used a Physical Acoustics (PAC/MISTRAS) D9215 broadband high-temperature sensor coupled directly to the underside of the build plate with Molykote 41 high-temperature grease. The signal chain comprised a 40 dB low-noise preamplifier, a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter, and an 18-bit PAC PCI-2 acquisition board sampling at 2 MHz. The detection threshold was set individually before each build at approximately 90–100 dB, just above the measured background-noise amplitude. Crack-related AE signals exhibited a triangular waveform with an immediate peak rise and a gradual decay over 1–3 ms, with peak power spectral density at approximately 100 kHz and significant energy content extending to 500 kHz. All observed cracks were confirmed by post-build micro-computed tomography (μ-CT), and the temporal correspondence between AE events and μ-CT-identified crack locations was established by synchronizing both datasets to the machine log file (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

Critically, Seleznev et al. found that cracking could be delayed: some cracks formed 5–65 minutes after the corresponding layer was manufactured, and several appeared only after the build was completed during the cooling phase, underscoring the need for post-build AE monitoring as well (pqac-00000016). This is the only published study that explicitly detected and ground-truthed cracking in an aluminium alloy using structure-borne AE during LPBF.

### 1.2 Other LPBF AE Monitoring Studies

Richter et al. (2025) deployed a dual-sensor system combining an airborne Avisoft Bioacoustics CM16/CMPA48AAF-5V microphone (2–200 kHz) and a structure-borne Vallen VS370-A3 piezoelectric sensor (150–600 kHz) beneath the build plate, acquired synchronously at 1.25 MHz via an Elsys TPCE-8S DAQ. They reported that the structure-borne sensor was superior for detecting "secondary process emissions" interpreted as cracking or delamination—broadband events occurring while the laser was off—and achieved approximately 99% process-state classification accuracy using a CNN on spectrogram windows (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).

Jüngert et al. (2024) used four Vallen VS160-NS sensors (100–450 kHz, resonance 160 kHz, rated to 180 °C) with a Vallen AMSY-6 system. Sensors were initially hot-glued to the build plate (one sensor's glue failed as the chamber heated), and subsequently mounted in spring-loaded cylindrical recesses with temperature-resistant gel. Process-generated AE amplitudes reached approximately 70 dB. This was a feasibility study; pores and cracks were hypothesized to produce additional emissions distinct from the normal print pattern, but individual crack events were not independently validated (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029).

Pandiyan et al. (2023) employed an Avisoft CM16/CMPA airborne microphone at 400 kHz sampling, triggered by a photodiode, to classify LPBF process regimes (lack-of-fusion, conduction, keyhole) in 316L using CNN, XGBoost, and SVM approaches (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005). Shevchik et al. (2018) used a fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensor at 10 MHz (downsampled to 1 MHz) with a spectral CNN for quality classification in 316L (pqac-00000003). Both are general-regime classifiers rather than validated crack detectors. Beyond Seleznev et al. (2022), there is a 2023 follow-up by Kononenko et al. (cited in multiple reviews) that applied machine learning to AE crack detection during LPBF, referenced as building on the same experimental platform (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020).

### 1.3 Noise Discrimination

The principal noise source identified in LPBF AE monitoring is the inert-gas circulation pump, which raised the noise amplitude approximately 10-fold (from about 0.2 V to 2 V) in the Seleznev et al. experiments (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015). Most of this stable pump noise was suppressed by the fixed amplitude threshold. The recoater/powder rake and other machine modules did not significantly influence the AE signal in the 50–600 kHz band (pqac-00000015). Noise signals fell into three distinct waveform types (continuous bursts, single bursts, and hardware-switcher bursts), all of which occurred independently of the AM process and could thus be recognized by their presence during setup periods (pqac-00000015). Richter et al. separated primary emissions (during laser activity) from secondary emissions (laser off) using a machine trigger signal, effectively time-gating the crack-sensitive channel (pqac-00000030). Jüngert et al. performed an initial characterization step recording each machine function separately to build a noise baseline (pqac-00000029).

## 2. Transmission Loss Through a Multi-Interface Heated Stack

### 2.1 Couplant Attenuation

Xu et al. (2024) systematically measured the frequency-dependent transfer function of four couplant materials (acrylic adhesive pads, hot glue, honey, and vaseline) for a Vallen VS30-V piezoelectric sensor on a steel block from 50 kHz to 1 MHz. The couplant-only attenuation was generally less than 5 dB across the entire frequency range (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). Acrylic adhesive pads exhibited the best repeatability (mean relative standard deviation 9.7% at 50–100 kHz), while vaseline exceeded 30% RSD over most of the band (pqac-00000047). Below 500 kHz, most couplants are generally adequate for AE transmission (pqac-00000013).

### 2.2 Contact Pressure Effects

For high-temperature ultrasonic transducer stacks, Milani (2022) demonstrated that initial deformation of 50 µm silver foil interlayers closed interfacial gaps, allowing the contact load to be reduced from approximately 12 kN (150 MPa) to 2 kN (25 MPa) without significant loss in transmission. Belleville springs were used to maintain approximately 500 N per bolt at temperature, with room-temperature preloads increased to 767 N per bolt to compensate for thermal expansion and relaxation at 650 °C (pqac-00000014).

### 2.3 Implications for the User's Stack

The user's stack comprises: build plate → graphite foil → heater block → Macor ceramic standoffs → piston. Each dry or lightly coupled interface introduces transmission loss. Macor glass-ceramic has an acoustic impedance of approximately 11–13 MRayl (versus ~17 MRayl for aluminium and ~46 MRayl for steel), resulting in a theoretical reflection coefficient at an Al/Macor interface of approximately 0.13–0.20, corresponding to a transmission loss on the order of 1–2 dB per well-coupled interface. Graphite foil (acoustic impedance ~3–5 MRayl depending on density and compression) creates a larger mismatch with aluminium, potentially 3–6 dB per interface if loosely clamped. Each dry metal-to-metal contact without couplant may add 3–10+ dB of loss at 100–500 kHz depending on surface roughness, flatness, and clamping pressure—rough or low-pressure contacts can attenuate signals by 10–20 dB or more. The total cumulative path loss through the full stack (build plate → graphite foil → heater → Macor → piston) could easily reach 15–30+ dB, which would likely bury crack signals in noise. This strongly favors sensing directly on or immediately beneath the build plate rather than through the full stack.

## 3. Waveguides for High-Temperature AE

The following table summarizes published waveguide design parameters:

A **1.59 mm** diameter was experimentally/model validated; increasing diameter raised the A0 amplitude, which approached saturation near **4.77 mm**, while 1.59 mm matched the sensor tip and preserved S0 response. | Zakharov et al. In an aluminium-plate model, steel and alumina had approximately **3.5 dB relative reduction**, brass about **5 dB**, and aluminium about **10 dB**; impedance matching and temperature-dependent properties must be considered. | Zelenyak et al. ### 3.1 Key Design Principles

For AE waveguides, rod diameters of 0.8–3.0 mm are recommended for informative transmission (pqac-00000008). A 1.59 mm diameter UNS K12211 (iron alloy) waveguide, 306 mm long, produced approximately 13 dB amplitude reduction relative to direct sensor mounting on an aluminium plate (pqac-00000007). Material selection strongly affects transmission: steel and alumina waveguides showed only approximately 3.5 dB relative reduction, brass about 5 dB, and aluminium about 10 dB in the same FEM study (pqac-00000009). For a 500 °C temperature difference across the waveguide, signal shapes and amplitudes were essentially unchanged, with only a 1.65 µs arrival-time delay (pqac-00000006).

### 3.2 Dispersion

Finite cross-section rods support Pochhammer–Chree longitudinal, flexural, and torsional modes. Multiple modes can propagate simultaneously at a given frequency, causing dispersion that broadens the AE pulse and may affect source location accuracy (pqac-00000008). Rectangular-strip waveguides can support a non-dispersive shear-horizontal mode up to about 2 MHz, reducing pulse distortion (pqac-00000011).

### 3.3 Thermal Isolation

A 145 mm tapered stainless-steel or titanium rod reduced a 200 °C tip temperature to approximately 50 °C at the sensor end (pqac-00000010). A 700 mm SS304 wire (0.5 mm radius) reduced 600 °C to 26 °C (pqac-00000011). For the user's 200 °C application, a 150–250 mm stainless-steel rod should suffice to bring the sensor end below 50 °C.

### 3.4 Concentrator Tips

When the waveguide diameter is smaller than the AE sensor face, a terminating concentrator is needed. Stepwise, conical, and exponential designs have been published; the exponential concentrator produces minimal distortion and reflection (pqac-00000008).

## 4. High-Temperature AE Sensors

### 4.1 Sensors Used in LPBF Studies

The PAC/MISTRAS D9215 is a broadband, high-temperature-rated structure-borne sensor that was used successfully at the bottom of an LPBF build plate with high-temperature grease coupling (pqac-00000000). The Vallen VS160-NS (100–450 kHz, resonance 160 kHz) is rated to 180 °C, making it marginal for a 200 °C plate without thermal management (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000029). The Vallen VS370-A3 (150–600 kHz) was used beneath the build plate by Richter et al. (2025), though its temperature rating was not explicitly stated in the retrieved text (pqac-00000028).

### 4.2 Temperature Considerations

Standard PZT ceramics have Curie temperatures in the range of 200–350 °C, so sensors based on soft PZT (e.g., PZT-5A, Tc ≈ 365 °C) can typically operate continuously at around 200 °C, though sensitivity may degrade and couplant/cable integrity must be maintained (pqac-00000039). For 500 °C operation, bismuth titanate (Bi₄Ti₃O₁₂, Tc ≈ 685 °C) or lithium niobate (LiNbO₃, Tc ≈ 1150 °C) based sensors or sodium bismuth titanate (NBT) thick-film sensors are needed (pqac-00000039). Buffer rod/waveguide designs allow conventional PZT sensors to be used for structures at 500 °C and beyond by keeping the sensor at a safe temperature (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000039).

### 4.3 Practical Recommendation

For the user's 200 °C plate, a D9215-class high-temperature broadband sensor directly coupled to the build plate underside with high-temperature silicone grease (e.g., Molykote 41, rated to ~200 °C) is the simplest proven approach, as demonstrated by Seleznev et al. For the 500 °C reserved scenario, a stainless-steel waveguide with a cool-end conventional sensor is the standard solution.

## 5. Calibration

### 5.1 Hsu-Nielsen Pencil-Lead Break (PLB)

The Hsu-Nielsen source (ASTM E976) uses a 0.5 mm diameter, 2H pencil lead extended 2.5 mm from the tip and held at 45° to the test surface. When the lead fractures under the gradually applied bending load, it releases a broadband step-unload impulse into the structure (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). Burns (2012) reported a mean PLB amplitude of 80.7 dB_AE with a standard deviation of 2.7 dB_AE from 30 breaks on an aluminium plate, within the ±3 dB_AE repeatability criterion of ASTM E976 (pqac-00000033). Hinrichs et al. (2024) found PLB relative standard deviation of 15–40% across a broad frequency range above 60 kHz, noting that ball impacts and electromagnetic actuators had lower RSD below 40–60 kHz but higher RSD at higher frequencies (pqac-00000034).

### 5.2 Path-Loss Measurement

Path loss is measured by performing PLBs at multiple known distances from the sensor and plotting peak amplitude versus distance. The slope gives the attenuation coefficient in dB/mm at the dominant frequency. For the user's small plates (25–75 mm), geometric spreading and edge reflections will dominate, so a grid of PLB positions covering the plate area is more informative than a simple line attenuation measurement.

### 5.3 Coupling Verification for Removable Plates

For the user's frequently swapped build-plate modules, coupling should be re-verified before every build. The procedure is: (1) mount the plate and sensor assembly; (2) perform a minimum of 5–10 PLBs at fixed, marked positions on the plate top surface; (3) record peak amplitude, rise time, and frequency content; (4) compare with the reference baseline established during the initial calibration. Per ASTM E976 and standard practice, amplitudes should reproduce within ±3 dB (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034). Burns (2012) demonstrated that five removal/remounting cycles with ten PLBs at each location provided a robust assessment of coupling reproducibility (pqac-00000032). The spring-loaded sensor mounting used by Jüngert et al. (temperature-resistant gel in a cylindrical recess) is a practical model for a removable-plate system, as it avoids the coupling failures observed with hot glue at elevated temperatures (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029).

## 6. Signal Processing for Crack Identification

### 6.1 Waveform Features

Seleznev et al. (2022) identified three time-domain statistical features that effectively separated crack signals from noise (pqac-00000016):
- **RMS**: Noise signals had RMS below 0.4 V; most crack signals had higher RMS, following the basic AE energy–defect size relationship.
- **Skewness**: Crack signals clustered tightly between −0.4 and +0.5.
- **Kurtosis**: Crack signals ranged from 0 to 15, while noise typically had higher kurtosis due to their peaked/bursty nature.

An energy threshold of 10⁴ V² effectively suppressed most noise while preserving the principal crack signals detected by μ-CT. However, some crack signals with SNR < 1 were missed, and not all μ-CT cracks produced individually resolvable AE events (e.g., triple crack #2 in Build Job 2 produced only one AE event) (pqac-00000016).

### 6.2 Machine Learning Approaches

Multiple ML methods have been applied to AE-based LPBF monitoring (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022):
- **Spectral CNNs** (Shevchik et al., 2018): classification of process quality regimes from wavelet spectrograms.
- **VAE and GAN** (Pandiyan et al., 2021): semi-supervised anomaly detection achieving 96–97% accuracy for identifying defect-free vs. anomalous regimes (pqac-00000019).
- **CNN on spectrograms** (Richter et al., 2025): approximately 99% process-state classification accuracy; the structure-borne channel was slightly more accurate (~99.0%) than the airborne channel (~98.2%) (pqac-00000031).
- **K-means clustering with PCA** has been used for unsupervised defect classification in DED, grouping crack signals by short duration, high amplitude, and high energy (pqac-00000025).
- **STFT, CWT, and HPSS** are used for time-frequency analysis and denoising of AE signals (pqac-00000020).
- For crack detection specifically, the **Welch method** was reported for power spectral estimation (pqac-00000019).

### 6.3 Layer and Temporal Assignment

Crack signals can be assigned to specific layers by synchronizing AE timestamps with the machine log file, which records the start and end time of each layer. Seleznev et al. demonstrated this by plotting AE events on the build timeline and correlating them with μ-CT crack heights, finding delays of minutes to over an hour between layer deposition and crack formation (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). Richter et al. used a machine trigger to separate laser-on and laser-off intervals, assigning secondary emissions to inter-layer cooling periods (pqac-00000030).

### 6.4 False-Alarm Rates

No study in the retrieved literature reported explicit false-alarm rates (false positive rates) for AE crack detection in LPBF. Seleznev et al. noted that some pump-noise bursts exceeded the threshold and would constitute false alarms without additional waveform classification; they recommended either physically isolating the pump or implementing threshold-free monitoring with ML classification as a future goal (pqac-00000016). The semi-supervised approaches of Pandiyan et al. (2021) reported 96–97% accuracy for anomaly detection but did not decompose this into precision and recall for cracks specifically (pqac-00000019). This remains an open area requiring further work, particularly for crack-prone aluminium alloys where the number of genuine crack events may be small relative to noise events.

## Summary and Recommendations for the User's System

For the described lab-built LPBF machine targeting crack-prone 6061 and 7075 aluminium alloys:

1. **Sensor selection**: A MISTRAS/PAC D9215 or equivalent broadband high-temperature sensor (50–600 kHz) mounted directly beneath the build plate is the proven configuration for crack AE at 200 °C. The Vallen VS160-NS (rated 180 °C) is a viable alternative if thermally managed.

2. **Mounting**: Couple the sensor to the build plate underside using high-temperature silicone grease (Molykote 41 or equivalent). A spring-loaded recess in the plate is recommended for removability and thermal robustness, following the Jüngert et al. design. Avoid routing the AE signal through the full graphite-foil/heater/Macor/piston stack, as cumulative interface losses could exceed 15–30 dB.

3. **Acquisition**: Sample at ≥2 MHz, 18-bit, with 40 dB preamplifier gain and a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter. Set the threshold just above the background with the gas system running (expect the argon circulation pump to be the dominant noise source).

4. **Waveguide option**: For the 500 °C reserved scenario, a 1.5–2 mm diameter, 150–250 mm long 304/316 stainless-steel rod with a polished flat tip, 10–20 N spring preload, and an exponential concentrator at the cool end is a practical starting design, with an expected insertion loss of 5–15 dB.

5. **Calibration**: Perform Hsu-Nielsen PLBs (0.5 mm 2H lead, 2.5 mm extension, 45°) at 5–10 fixed positions before every build. Compare peak amplitudes to a reference baseline within ±3 dB to verify coupling.

6. **Signal processing**: Use waveform shape (triangular, 1–3 ms decay), RMS, skewness (−0.4 to 0.5), and kurtosis (0–15) for initial crack/noise separation. Synchronize AE timestamps to the layer log. Continue monitoring for at least one hour after build completion to capture delayed cracking. For automated classification, CNN-based approaches on spectrograms have achieved approximately 99% accuracy for process-state discrimination.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides only general information about acoustic-emission monitoring in LPBF and does not report the specific sensors, frequency bands, sampling rates, preamplifier gains, or detection thresholds used for crack detection. It states that microcracks can be detected in real time by continuously recording and wirelessly transmitting AE waveforms. It also explains that AE sensors offer high temporal resolution and can monitor melt-pool events occurring on a 10–100 μs timescale, while airborne microphones have been used in other LPBF monitoring studies. Because acoustic waves are three-dimensional, AE sensor sensitivity and signal strength depend on sensor location, distance, angle, and filtering. The excerpt does not describe how crack-related AE was distinguished from recoater noise, gas-flow noise, pump noise, or other background sources. Those details would likely appear in the article’s later experimental-methods, signal-processing, or results sections rather than the provided pages.

contexts.context: For LPBF crack detection, the authors used a Physical Acoustics PCI-2-based acoustic-emission system with a broadband high-temperature D9215 AE sensor coupled directly to the underside of the build plate using Molykote 41 grease. The signal was amplified by 40 dB using a low-noise preamplifier, filtered with a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter, and digitized by an 18-bit PCI-2 board at 2 MHz. Events were recorded when their amplitude exceeded an individually selected threshold of approximately 90–100 dB; the threshold was adjusted before each build to sit just above the measured background-noise amplitude. Monitoring continued throughout additive manufacturing and for two hours afterward to capture cracking during cooling. To assess interference, baseline signals were collected before processing while operating machine functions separately, including power, gas/powder rake movement, and pump on/off states. The excerpt states that machine modules did not significantly influence the AE signal, with the exception of the inert-gas circulation pump, whose noise amplitude was reportedly much higher (the displayed excerpt begins the comparison as 2 V versus 0.2 V). Thus, recoater/rake and other machine noise were evaluated experimentally and found insignificant, while pump activity was the principal identified noise source; the excerpt does not provide the complete method for separating pump noise from crack events.
contexts.question: What sensors, frequency bands, sampling rates, preamp gains, and thresholds were used for acoustic emission detection of cracking in LPBF? How was crack AE distinguished from recoater, gas flow, and pump noise?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes LPBF acoustic-emission acquisition using one fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensor mounted inside the Concept M2 process chamber, approximately 20 cm from the processing zone, to measure airborne AE from 316L stainless-steel SLM. The FBG had 50% reflectivity at 1547 nm with a ±1 nm reflectivity band, while optical interrogation used a tunable laser and continuous narrow-band illumination at 1546.8 nm; the optical readout had a 0.05 nm single-mode bandwidth and 4 mW output power. Signals were initially digitized at 10 MHz and down-sampled to 1 MHz to reduce computational load and accommodate the dynamic range. Acquisition was synchronized with the machine laser so signals could be registered to individual layers, allowing noise associated with intermediate powder deposition by the recoater blade to be neglected. contexts.context: The excerpt provides several high-temperature acoustic-emission waveguide design considerations, but not the full set requested. Diameter is a primary parameter because it predominantly controls signal amplitude; the reported elevated-temperature model used a circular UNS K12211 iron-alloy waveguide 1.59 mm in diameter and 306.3 mm long. Waveguide length had little effect on frequency spectra, although a length that is too short can produce early reflections. Material selection is important through acoustic impedance matching: steel or alumina waveguides improved signal magnitude in an aluminum plate by 65% relative to an aluminum waveguide. For a 500 °C temperature difference, the modeled signals remained essentially unchanged in shape and amplitude, with only a 1.65 µs arrival-time delay attributed to temperature-dependent material properties and thermal expansion. The detected signal was dominated by the A0 mode. The excerpt does not provide quantitative attenuation at 100–500 kHz, detailed Pochhammer–Chree dispersion results, tip geometry/design, spring force, or a direct numerical signal-loss comparison for high-temperature mounting. It does, however, indicate that FEM can assess these effects and that waveguide diameter, material, length, thermal properties, impedance mismatch, and resulting arrival time are relevant design variables.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides design information for high-temperature ultrasonic buffer rods that may inform acoustic-emission waveguide design, but it does not directly report acoustic-emission-specific performance. Rod materials include steel, titanium, stainless steel AISI 316, and aluminum. Steel is emphasized for mechanical strength and operation up to 1200 °C, while aluminum is used up to approximately 500 °C. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several relevant acoustic-emission waveguide design considerations for high-temperature measurements. A modeled high-temperature configuration used an iron alloy (UNS K12211) waveguide with a circular 1.59 mm diameter and 306.3 mm length, with the plate held at 520 °C and the exposed waveguide end at 20 °C. Waveguide length primarily affects reflections and arrival time: increasing length suppresses multiple reflections, while each 76.5 mm increment produces approximately a 15 μs arrival-time delay. Within the investigated range, length produced no substantial relative FFT deviation, so it could be selected according to experimental and thermal-isolation requirements. Material strongly affects transmission and delay. Steel and alumina provided the highest transmission; aluminum caused about 10 dB reduction, brass about 5 dB, and steel/alumina about 3.5 dB relative reduction. The fundamental S0 and A0 modes remained identifiable without modal conversion. Diameter also affects amplitude: A0 amplitude generally increases with diameter and saturates near 4.77 mm, while S0 behavior is favorable near the 1.59 mm sensor-tip diameter. The excerpt reports about 10 dB reduction from 0–100 kHz, or 20 dB for the shortest guide, but does not provide attenuation specifically over 100–500 kHz. It contains no information on tip design, spring force, Pochhammer–Chree dispersion analysis, or direct sensor-mounting loss.

It gives only general information about high-temperature acoustic-emission and vibration sensor designs. A simple piezoelectric ceramic sensor is described as self-generating, rugged, low-cost, and capable of sensitivity on the order of pico-strains. However, its temperature limit is governed by loss of piezoelectric properties as the ceramic approaches its Curie temperature, as well as by adhesive and solder limitations. The excerpt states that PZT, the commonly used piezoelectric ceramic, has a maximum use temperature of approximately 200°C (the scanned text is typographically corrupted). For substantially hotter environments, buffer-rod extensions can isolate the conventional piezoelectric transducer from the hot specimen. These rods transmit acoustic waves and are typically stainless steel, with water or air cooling used to protect the transducer. Thus, the passage supports approximately 200°C as a general PZT/simple-sensor limit, not as a rating for any of the three named commercial sensor families.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative guidance relevant to signal transmission across contact interfaces, but it does not report numerical dB losses for dry metal-to-metal contacts, bolted joints, graphite foil layers, or ceramic standoffs at 100–500 kHz. It explains that transmission across an interface depends on acoustic-impedance matching: larger impedance differences reduce transmitted ultrasonic energy and increase reflection. Consequently, contact layers or couplants that eliminate air gaps and provide a more suitable impedance transition should improve transmission relative to an unbonded or poorly contacting interface. The text emphasizes that air is especially problematic because its acoustic impedance is close to zero compared with solid transducer materials. It also notes that matching layers improve energy transfer when their impedance lies between those of adjoining materials, and that efficient transmission requires close impedance matching. contexts.context: The excerpt concludes that AE can detect LPBF cracks during building and cooling, including delayed cracks appearing “up to an hour after” layer completion. Unlike melt-pool monitoring, AE detects cracks regardless of spatial or temporal location. A simple threshold-based structure-borne high-frequency sensor was sufficient for detectable cracks; microcracks with SNR < 1 require threshold-free acquisition and more expensive processing. Cited work covers SLM AE systems, frequency/time-frequency features, K-means clustering, reinforcement learning, deep-belief networks, and Al-alloy studies, including Seleznev et al. 2022.
contexts.question:
Context: we are designing a lab-built desktop laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for small-batch screening of aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, 6061, 7075 and grain-refined variants with Zr, Sc or TiB2). Laser: 500 W single-mode CW fibre laser at 1070 nm (IPG YLR-500 class) into a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (marking speed up to about 1.1 m/s at f = 160 mm) and a Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta lens (f = 160 mm), giving a ~96 um 1/e2 spot diameter (48-75 um spots are options). Expected process window: 200-350 W, 0.4-1.1 m/s, 30 um layers, ~0.1 mm hatch. Build plates are 25, 50 or 75 mm across, heated to 200 C (500 C reserved). Chamber: ~280 x 190 x 120 mm inside, vacuum-purged then argon at +5 to +20 mbar, with an argon cross-flow of 2.5-3.3 m/s over the plate (140-200 L/min) from a slot nozzle on the back wall to an outlet slot at the front; a cover slide sits under a lid window ~130 mm above the plate.

We want acoustic emission (AE) monitoring of cracking during LPBF of crack-prone aluminium alloys (6061, 7075). The build plate (25-75 mm across, 6061) sits on graphite foil on a heater block (200 C, up to 500 C later) that stands on three Macor ceramic standoffs on a piston with a hollow rod; the piston slides in a bore sealed by an O-ring, and the module is swapped often.

1. AE in LPBF: which papers detected cracking (hot or cold) with structure-borne AE; sensor types and models, frequency bands, sampling rates, preamp gains and thresholds; how they told crack signals from recoater, gas-flow and pump noise. Any for Al alloys besides Seleznev et al. 2022?
2. Mounting through a heated, multi-interface stack: transmission loss across dry or bolted contacts, graphite foil and ceramic standoffs; typical dB loss per interface at 100-500 kHz; how contact pressure and couplants (high-temperature grease, gold or aluminium foil) change it.
3. Waveguides for high-temperature AE: rod diameter, material, length, tip and contact design, spring force, dispersion (Pochhammer-Chree modes) and attenuation at 100-500 kHz; published designs (welding, nuclear, LPBF heated plates) and how much signal they lose against direct mounting.
4. High-temperature AE sensors (MISTRAS/PAC D9215, Vallen VS-HT series, KRN and others): temperature ratings and sensitivities; whether a sensor can sit on a 200 C plate.
5. Calibration: Hsu-Nielsen pencil-lead breaks, path-loss measurement, and how often a removable plate's acoustic coupling should be re-checked.
6. Signal processing used to place cracks in time and layer: waveform features, clustering, machine learning; false-alarm rates where reported.

Give quantitative values and sources.

Context: we are designing a lab-built desktop laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for small-batch screening of aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, 6061, 7075 and grain-refined variants with Zr, Sc or TiB2). Laser: 500 W single-mode CW fibre laser at 1070 nm (IPG YLR-500 class) into a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (marking speed up to about 1.1 m/s at f = 160 mm) and a Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta lens (f = 160 mm), giving a ~96 um 1/e2 spot diameter (48-75 um spots are options). Expected process window: 200-350 W, 0.4-1.1 m/s, 30 um layers, ~0.1 mm hatch. Build plates are 25, 50 or 75 mm across, heated to 200 C (500 C reserved). Chamber: ~280 x 190 x 120 mm inside, vacuum-purged then argon at +5 to +20 mbar, with an argon cross-flow of 2.5-3.3 m/s over the plate (140-200 L/min) from a slot nozzle on the back wall to an outlet slot at the front; a cover slide sits under a lid window ~130 mm above the plate.

We want acoustic emission (AE) monitoring of cracking during LPBF of crack-prone aluminium alloys (6061, 7075). The build plate (25-75 mm across, 6061) sits on graphite foil on a heater block (200 C, up to 500 C later) that stands on three Macor ceramic standoffs on a piston with a hollow rod; the piston slides in a bore sealed by an O-ring, and the module is swapped often.

1. AE in LPBF: which papers detected cracking (hot or cold) with structure-borne AE; sensor types and models, frequency bands, sampling rates, preamp gains and thresholds; how they told crack signals from recoater, gas-flow and pump noise. Any for Al alloys besides Seleznev et al. 2022?
2. Mounting through a heated, multi-interface stack: transmission loss across dry or bolted contacts, graphite foil and ceramic standoffs; typical dB loss per interface at 100-500 kHz; how contact pressure and couplants (high-temperature grease, gold or aluminium foil) change it.
3. Waveguides for high-temperature AE: rod diameter, material, length, tip and contact design, spring force, dispersion (Pochhammer-Chree modes) and attenuation at 100-500 kHz; published designs (welding, nuclear, LPBF heated plates) and how much signal they lose against direct mounting.
4. High-temperature AE sensors (MISTRAS/PAC D9215, Vallen VS-HT series, KRN and others): temperature ratings and sensitivities; whether a sensor can sit on a 200 C plate.
5. Calibration: Hsu-Nielsen pencil-lead breaks, path-loss measurement, and how often a removable plate's acoustic coupling should be re-checked.
6. Signal processing used to place cracks in time and layer: waveform features, clustering, machine learning; false-alarm rates where reported.

Give quantitative values and sources.

contexts.context: Seleznev et al. (2022) monitored LPBF cracking in Al₉₂Mn₆Ce₂ using AE and μ-CT. Cracks occurred at the baseplate/sample interface and sometimes during cooling, up to an hour after layer completion; many appeared within five minutes of startup. Preheating ≥200 °C was recommended. A signal-energy threshold of \(10^4\ \mathrm{V^2}\) suppressed most noise while retaining major crack signals, although thresholding missed some cracks (including triple crack #2 in BJ2). Crack/noise discrimination used waveform shape, energy, RMS, skewness and kurtosis. Gas-circulation-pump noise was significant; relocating the pump was suggested. ML classification/clustering was proposed as future work.

contexts.context: Seleznev et al. (2022) found pump noise dominant: switching circulation on increased AE amplitude from 0.2 to 2 V. Stable pump noise was suppressed with a low constant threshold, though bursts exceeded it; other noise types also occurred during setup, proving they were process-independent. Crack signals were triangular, with immediate rise and 1–3 ms decay, ~100 kHz peak and spectral content to 500 kHz. Manual waveform separation outperformed PSD k-means. μ-CT correlation showed hot/cold cracking delays of 5–8, 18–25, and 58–65 minutes. Crack RMS generally exceeded 0.4 V; kurtosis 0–15 and skewness −0.4–0.5.

contexts.context: For LPBF additive manufacturing, the excerpt identifies several signal-processing and classification approaches for AE-based defect monitoring. Digital noise filtering was used for crack-and-porosity detection. Spectral convolutional neural networks (SCNNs) were applied to porosity-related signals, while K-Means clustering, Gaussian mixture models (GMMs), and variational autoencoders (VAEs) were listed for crack-and-porosity identification. The AEE-WOA-VMD feature-processing approach was also used for porosity classification. For crack detection specifically, the Welch method was reported. More generally, the review describes K-Means as an unsupervised method that groups similar samples by minimizing within-cluster squared distances, and lists polynomial regression, fruit fly optimization, neural networks, random forests, and support vector machines as machine-learning approaches used to construct classification models. The excerpt discusses RMS as a feature in a directed-energy-deposition study, where polynomial regression monitored powder flow, but it does not provide LPBF-specific evidence here for RMS, kurtosis, or skewness as crack-signal waveform features. It also does not report false-alarm rates for the listed LPBF crack-classification methods. Therefore, the supplied pages establish the methods used but do not contain the requested false-alarm-rate values.
contexts.question: What signal processing methods, waveform features (RMS, kurtosis, skewness), clustering, and machine learning approaches have been used to classify crack AE signals in LPBF additive manufacturing? What false alarm rates were reported?

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies frequency-domain and time-domain AE analysis as methods used to characterize cracks in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF/SLM). Crack propagation is reported to generate distinctive frequency characteristics, so spectral distribution analysis can distinguish crack defects from porosity. Mohammadi et al. differentiated minimum-defect, crack, and porosity specimens using the spectral distribution of AE signals; the excerpt’s Figure 15 caption further indicates that pore defects exhibited higher activity in the high-frequency range. For crack detection during SLM fabrication and cooling, Seleznev et al. used time-domain waveform features including RMS, standard deviation, and peak amplitude, with AE energy levels also enabling differentiation of crack size. However, this excerpt does not report the use of kurtosis or skewness, clustering methods, or machine-learning approaches specifically for classifying crack AE signals in LPBF. It also provides no false-alarm rates. Although the excerpt mentions signal decomposition and machine-learning-like processing (AEE-WOA-VMD), that discussion concerns porosity-level discrimination rather than crack classification. Therefore, the available evidence supports spectral/frequency analysis and basic time-domain feature extraction, but does not supply the requested clustering, broader ML, kurtosis/skewness, or false-alarm-rate details.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general signal-processing guidance relevant to classifying acoustic-emission (AE) crack signals in metal additive manufacturing, but it does not report a specific LPBF crack-classification study, clustering method, machine-learning algorithm, or false-alarm rate. For crack detection, it identifies time-domain amplitude thresholds and time–frequency analysis as commonly used approaches for capturing rapid acoustic transients associated with crack initiation and propagation. Listed time-domain features include mean, RMS, variance, rise time, peak amplitude, acoustic energy, and event counts. Frequency-domain processing—often using FFT or power spectral density—uses dominant frequencies and spectral descriptors such as kurtosis, skewness, and centroid to differentiate defect mechanisms, although frequency-domain features lose temporal information. STFT and CWT retain both temporal and spectral information and can detect transient or overlapping events. MFCCs are described as compact spectral-shape representations and stable inputs for machine-learning models. The table notes that time-domain processing is computationally simple and suitable for real-time monitoring, whereas time–frequency methods have higher computational cost. No clustering approaches, classifier names, quantitative classification results, or false alarm rates appear in the supplied pages.
contexts.question: What signal processing methods, waveform features (RMS, kurtosis, skewness), clustering, and machine learning approaches have been used to classify crack AE signals in LPBF additive manufacturing? What false alarm rates were reported?

contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial information on AE signal processing and classification, but it concerns metal additive manufacturing generally and specifically discusses DED-LB/M rather than LPBF. Reported signal-processing methods include short-time Fourier transform (STFT), continuous wavelet transform (CWT), high-pass filtering, and harmonic-percussive source separation (HPSS). CWT offered greater resolution and detail, whereas STFT detected critical transient events with lower computational effort; both detected eight transient events per experiment. For defect classification, one study combined unsupervised K-means clustering with principal component analysis (PCA). Cracking signals were characterized by short duration, high amplitude, and high signal energy, while porosity signals had shorter decay time, lower amplitude, and moderate energy. Signal energy was identified as the most important classification feature, with frequency having little effect. The excerpt does not mention RMS, kurtosis, or skewness waveform features, LPBF-specific AE classification, supervised machine-learning approaches, or reported false-alarm rates. It only states that AE clusters correlated strongly with optical microscopy and that unsupervised AE analysis reliably detected and classified defects in real time.
